items.title: QuiX Quantum Leads National Mission to Develop 100+ Qubit Photonic Quantum Computer
items.summary:
Insider Brief

QuiX Quantum will lead a national mission under Phase II of the PhotonDelta National Growth Fund programme to develop the technology foundations for a universal photonic quantum computer with more than 100 qubits.

The project runs from January 2026 to December 2028 and brings together QuiX Quantum and nine Dutch industrial and academic partners to develop twelve components across the photonic quantum computing stack.

The work targets lower optical loss, improved photon sources, advanced detection, faster control electronics and more manufacturable chips, with the results intended to support QuiX Quantum ‘s fault-tolerant computing roadmap.

PRESS RELEASE — QuiX Quantum , a Dutch-German developer of universal photonic quantum computers, has been the Photonic Quantum Computing Mission awarded funding under Phase II of the PhotonDelta National Growth Fund (NGF) Integrated Photonics Programme.

QuiX Quantum and seven partners awarded the photonic quantum computing mission to solve the challenges of scaling.

Running from January 2026 through December 2028, the mission, “Delivery of a 100+ Qubit Universal Quantum Computer”, brings together QuiX Quantum and nine Dutch industrial and academic partners. Together they will develop and integrate twelve deliverables covering the quantum photonic stack, from low-loss chips and photon sources to detection, control electronics, packaging and manufacturing.

items.title: QuEra, Harvard and Anthropic Use AI to Reduce Quantum Circuit Resource Requirements
items.summary:
Insider Brief

Researchers from QuEra Computing , Harvard University and Anthropic used Claude to design quantum circuits that reduce gate counts and qubit requirements across seven of eight computational building blocks.

The research reported a 12-fold reduction in Toffoli gates for a Reed-Solomon decoder, a 9.9-fold reduction in combined resources for a Coulomb potential calculation, and a 39-fold reduction for a fixed-point Gaussian function.

The team also developed a new reversible modular inversion approach that offers additional trade-offs between gate counts and qubit requirements.

PRESS RELEASE — QuEra Computing , the leader in fault-tolerant quantum computing, today highlighted research with Harvard University and Anthropic showing that AI can design quantum circuits that require fewer computational resources. The findings show how advances in algorithm design could expand what future fault-tolerant quantum computers can accomplish with a given hardware capacity.

The research preprint, “Discovering state-of-the-art quantum circuits with large language models” (arXiv:2610.22367), examines eight computational building blocks used in larger quantum algorithms. In seven, AI-designed circuits reduced both gate counts and qubit requirements relative to the corresponding baseline designs. In the eighth, the search found a new approach that offers additional choices between qubit requirements and gate counts. The research, reflecting an industry-first collaboration of AI and Quantum market leaders, was led by Andi Gu as part of Anthropic ‘s STEM Fellows Program, with Alek Kemeny of Anthropic, Susanne Yelin of Harvard , and Mikhail Lukin of Harvard and QuEra .

Useful quantum computing arrives where two curves meet. One is hardware capability, which rises as machines gain more qubits and more reliable operations. The other is the resources useful algorithms require, which fall as those algorithms are made more efficient. Progress on either curve moves the meeting point earlier; progress on both can bring valuable applications within reach sooner. This research addresses the second curve.

items.title: Draft EU Quantum Act Would Favor European Suppliers, Set Computing and Security Targets
items.summary:
Insider Brief

A draft EU Quantum Act would coordinate European quantum research, manufacturing and commercialization while generally reserving strategic projects and public procurement for EU-controlled suppliers and qualifying international partners.

The draft targets approximately 100 error-corrected logical qubits per system by 2030 or soon after and proposes shared infrastructure for quantum computing, communications, sensing and timing.

The proposal would introduce quantum-safe purchasing requirements for critical sectors, with funding dependent on future EU programmes, national contributions and private investment.

If Winston Churchill were here today, he might say an “ion curtain” is descending across the Continent.

Europe’s proposed Quantum Act would generally reserve public purchases of quantum technology and participation in strategic projects for EU-controlled companies, while leaving a door open to qualifying international partners, according to a draft of the document obtained by The Quantum Insider.

According to the document, the act would establish a common framework for European quantum research, engineering and industrial development, requiring member states to align national strategies with shared priorities. It would also introduce purchasing requirements for quantum-safe security in critical sectors and set ambitions for error-corrected computing and cross-border quantum networks.

items.title: Commission on U.S. Quantum Primacy Urges Sustained Investment to Turn Quantum Discovery Into American Advantage
items.summary:
Insider Brief

A preliminary report from the Commission on U.S. Quantum Primacy calls for expanding U.S. quantum leadership from research into deployment, manufacturing and industrial scale.

The report warns that China’s public investment, manufacturing capacity and supply chains could help it scale quantum technologies faster than the United States.

Priorities include sustained research funding, coordinated hardware and software development, post-quantum security, foundry access and workforce training, with implementation recommendations due in spring 2027.

PRESS RELEASE — The Commission on U.S. Quantum Primacy (CUSP), convened by the Special Competitive Studies Project (SCSP), released today its preliminary report, Defining the American Quantum Era , a strategy argument for why the United States must move beyond scientific leadership in quantum and build the capacity to deploy and manufacture quantum technologies at scale. The Commission is co-chaired by U.S. Sen.Todd Young (R-IN), U.S. Sen. Ben Ray Luján (D-NM), and Ylli Bajraktari, president of SCSP.

The report warns that America’s strengths in research, software and private investment will not automatically become leadership in deployment or industrial scale. The U.S. currently holds an edge in quantum research and in deployed quantum computing systems, but that position varies across the quantum technologies. China has made quantum a strategic priority, backing it with significant public investment, and is moving from demonstration to infrastructure in areas like quantum networking. Supply chain and manufacturing advantages, paired with a well-funded R&D base, could allow China to scale quantum innovation faster than the United States.

“Leadership in quantum will not be decided by who publishes the most papers or reaches a single milestone first,” said Bajraktari. “It will be decided by who turns quantum discoveries into deployed, manufactured, trusted capabilities. This preliminary report lays out what the United States must get right across discovery, development, deployment, and scale, and the window to act is limited.”

items.title: Xanadu and HyperLight Reduce Photonic Switch Loss to 7 mdB
items.summary:
Insider Brief

Xanadu and HyperLight have demonstrated an optical switch insertion loss of 7 millidecibels (mdB) using HyperLight ‘s thin-film lithium niobate (TFLN) Chiplet platform, improving on their previous 20 mdB result from 2025.

The new result was achieved on a high-volume wafer manufacturing line and is intended to reduce photon signal loss, a key challenge in scaling photonic quantum computers.

The companies say the improvement could support more efficient manufacturing and the development of larger photonic quantum systems, with potential applications across data centre infrastructure.

PRESS RELEASE — Xanadu Quantum Technologies Limited (“ Xanadu ”; NASDAQ/TSX: XNDU), a leading photonic quantum computing company, in collaboration with HyperLight Corporation , a leading thin-film lithium niobate (TFLN) photonics company, today announced a significant hardware performance milestone using TFLN technology, reducing optical switch insertion loss to 7 millidecibels (mdB). This achievement represents a nearly threefold improvement over Xanadu and HyperLight ’s previous breakthrough of 20 mdB in 2025, drastically reducing qubit signal degradation, which is one of the most critical challenges in scaling quantum computers. This industry-leading achievement was demonstrated using a high-volume wafer manufacturing line on HyperLight’s TFLN Chiplet platform and shows excellent yield and repeatability.

“This notable switch insertion loss milestone indicates that Xanadu ’s quantum-compatible switches are ready to ramp to production, bringing scalable quantum hardware and utility-scale quantum computing (USQC) one step closer to reality,” said Dr. Christian Weedbrook, Founder and Chief Executive Officer of Xanadu. “For Xanadu, minimizing optical loss is one of the most critical factors in making fault-tolerant photonic quantum computing commercially viable, and innovative partners like HyperLight are key to our go-to-market strategy.”

Optical switches are vital components in photonic quantum computers, responsible for routing light particles (photons) that carry quantum information. Because quantum signals cannot be conventionally amplified without destroying fragile quantum states, ultra-low insertion loss is paramount. Lowering switch loss preserves quantum state fidelity, prevents lost qubits, and allows photonic networks to scale efficiently without requiring exponential increases in laser power or physical hardware redundancy.

items.title: Gartner Names IonQ a Market Shaper in Quantum Computing
items.summary:
Insider Brief

IonQ has been named a Market Shaper in Gartner’s inaugural Emerging Market Quadrant for Quantum Computing, which assesses vendors in the emerging quantum computing market.

Gartner describes Market Shapers as vendors with experience delivering and supporting systems in commercial environments, while IonQ says the recognition reflects its full-stack platform and progress toward fault-tolerant quantum computing.

The announcement follows several IonQ milestones, including advancement to Stage C of DARPA’s Quantum Benchmarking Initiative, $7.5 million in follow-on funding from the Air Force Research Laboratory, and planned Superion 256 deployments.

PRESS RELEASE — IonQ (NYSE: IONQ), the world’s leading full-stack quantum platform and foundry, today announced it has been positioned as a Market Shaper in the inaugural Gartner® Emerging Market Quadrant for Quantum Computing. IonQ appears in the Market Shapers quadrant of the graphic above.

In the report, Gartner states: “Market Shapers have proven their ability to reliably deliver and support cutting-edge systems in commercial environments, making them generally less risky bets for technology buyers seeking transformation.” Gartner also states: “These vendors are low-risk, high-impact leaders of the emerging quantum market.”

“We’re honored by this recognition from Gartner. We feel this is a significant validation of what our team has built,” said Niccolo de Masi, Chairman and CEO of IonQ . “It reflects years of work on our full-stack quantum platform that customers are using today as well as our consistent execution toward our fault tolerant roadmap. Quantum has now moved out of the lab with accelerating real world use cases and commercial deployment. We believe IonQ is building the quantum ecosystem and setting the industry standard.”

items.title: D-Wave Revenue Rises 21% as Customer Deployments Expand And CHIPS Agreement Advances
items.summary:
Insider Brief

D-Wave reported third-quarter revenue of $4.5 million, up 21% from a year earlier, and $38.3 million in contracted revenue remaining to be recognized.

Nine-month bookings increased 611% to $37.4 million, although third-quarter bookings declined 19% to $1.9 million.

The company highlighted customer deployments and conditional CHIPS funding, while operating expenses increased and gross margin declined.

D-Wave Quantum reported a 21% increase in third-quarter revenue as professional services and cloud access sales grew, alongside customer deployments and a federal agreement supporting development of its next quantum computers.

Revenue reached $4.5 million for the quarter ended Sept. 30, according to the company’s earnings release . Nine-month bookings increased 611% to $37.4 million, although quarterly bookings fell 19% to $1.9 million. The company said larger transactions can cause substantial quarterly variation.

“From Seoul to Como to Washington, we are seeing growing interest in D-Wave ’s differentiated dual-platform approach and a determination to put our quantum computing technology to work today,” Dr. Alan Baratz, CEO of D-Wave said in the statement. “Our triple-digit increase in year-to-date bookings and robust pipeline reinforce our confidence in the opportunity ahead. We are expanding our commercial reach and executing on both our annealing and gate-model roadmaps with a clear objective: to lead this industry in technical and scientific innovation, measurable customer value and growth.”

items.title: Horizon Quantum Reports Q3 2026 Financial Results
items.summary:
Insider Brief

Horizon Quantum reported Q3 2026 net income of $33.4 million, including a $43.1 million non-cash gain from the remeasurement of warrant-related derivative liabilities, while its operating loss widened to $10.5 million.

The company reported an adjusted EBITDA loss of $6.3 million, compared with $3 million in Q3 2025, and ended the quarter with $102.8 million in cash and cash equivalents.

Business developments included pulse-level integration with OQC’s 32-qubit Toshiko processor, multiplexed characterisation on a processor with more than 100 qubits, and a non-binding agreement to acquire Singapore-based Entropica Labs for an anticipated $27 million in shares.

PRESS RELEASE — Horizon Quantum Holdings Ltd. (Nasdaq: HQ) (“Horizon Quantum,” “Horizon,” or “the Company”), a pioneer of software infrastructure for quantum applications, today reported financial results for the fiscal third quarter ended September 30, 2026 (“Q3 2026”).

Third Quarter 2026 Financial and Business Highlights (all figures approximate and presented in USD):

Horizon Quantum and Oxford Quantum Circuits (“OQC”) announce successful pulse-level integration.

items.title: IBM Selects Four Organisations for AI and Quantum Workforce Programme
items.summary:
Insider Brief

IBM has selected four organisations for its 2026 Impact Accelerator cohort, providing technology and expertise to support education and workforce development in AI and emerging fields such as quantum computing.

The selected organisations will work on projects covering AI and digital literacy for educators, quantum and AI readiness in Colorado, job-seeker support in Latin America, and career guidance for students in India.

The Colorado Office of Economic Development and International Trade will work with IBM on AI-enabled economic development tools and wider access to quantum resources, including IBM Qiskit.

PRESS RELEASE — IBM (NYSE: IBM ) today announced four organizations selected for the new education and workforce development cohort of the IBM Impact Accelerator , a pro bono social innovation program that provides grants of IBM technology and expertise to help nonprofit and government organizations to design, develop and scale technology-enabled solutions to challenges facing communities around the world.

AI is changing the skills employers need and how students and workers navigate the labor market. According to the World Economic Forum , more than one in three young workers globally are employed in occupations with medium to high exposure to AI-driven task change, underscoring how quickly entry-level career pathways are evolving.

Emerging fields such as quantum computing are also creating new demand for specialized skills and expertise. Together, these shifts are putting new pressure on education and workforce systems around the world. The new cohort addresses that shift at different points along the education-to-workforce journey.

items.title: Diraq Deploys Silicon Spin Quantum Computer Inside a Commercial Data Center
items.summary:
Insider Brief

Diraq has installed an eight-qubit silicon spin quantum computer at Equinix’s Sydney data center, describing it as the first commercial data center deployment of the technology.

The system consumes less than 20 kilowatts and occupies 170 square feet, with Diraq targeting an upgrade to as many as 256 qubits within a year.

Diraq’s new Quantum at Work report examines potential applications, including modeling suggesting a 10-percentage-point increase in clinical trial success rates could save about $600 million per medicine.

PRESS RELEASE — Quantum computing pioneer  Diraq has installed the world’s first silicon spin quantum computer inside a commercial data center, now live at Equinix (Nasdaq: EQIX) in Sydney, Australia. As quantum computing moves into the everyday infrastructure that businesses rely on, Diraq is also launching Quantum at Work , a new report exploring how the technology could be put to work on some of the world’s hardest problems including medicine discovery.

“We are now at a point where quantum computing can start to reach industries and the people they serve,” said Andrew Dzurak, CEO and Founder of Diraq. “That shift matters more than any single milestone, because it changes what’s possible for every field quantum touches, from medicine to materials to logistics. Our silicon spin approach is what puts that within reach in five years, not decades. It gives us a manufacturing path already proven at industrial scale, a cost curve that improves as we add qubits, and a system designed to run inside today’s existing computing infrastructure.”

A new benchmark for commercial deployment

items.title: Chiral waveguide model for error-correctable quantum computation
items.summary:
We develop a first-principles framework connecting microscopic waveguide scattering to quantum error correction and algorithmic performance. For polarization-encoded single photons interacting with an ensemble of two-level atoms in a chiral waveguide, we derive an effective polarization quantum channel by tracing out the frequency degree of freedom.

Using this channel as the physical noise model for a rotated planar code, we observe threshold behavior as the number of atoms $N$ and the atom-waveguide coupling strength $Γ$ are varied. An asymptotic analysis of the microscopic scattering model explains the threshold scaling with $NΓ/σ$, where $σ$ is the photon spectral bandwidth.

For identical, lossless atoms with symmetric real coupling and a photon spectrum centered at resonance, the effective noise is strongly biased toward $X$ errors. We then incorporate the resulting logical errors into quantum phase estimation and demonstrate that the noise bias can guide circuit design.

In particular, a Hadamard-basis implementation reduces sensitivity to the dominant error, improving algorithmic performance.

items.title: Adaptive Quantization Preserves Fast Rates for TD Learning over Rate-Limited Channels
items.summary:
Motivated by reinforcement learning subject to communication constraints, we study a policy evaluation problem with linear function approximation over a rate-limited channel. In our setup, an agent interacting with an unknown environment (modeled as a Markov Decision Process) transmits quantized estimates of a temporal-difference (TD) learning update direction to a server over a finite-capacity channel.

Our goal is to investigate to what extent one can preserve the statistical convergence rates achievable when the channel has infinite capacity. To that end, we propose a new algorithm called Batched Adaptively Quantized TD (BAQ-TD), which uses batching to reduce the variance of the transmitted information, and adaptive quantization to encode innovations.

We prove a high-probability finite-time error bound for BAQ-TD, and show that, above a certain finite channel capacity, BAQ-TD preserves the convergence rate of unquantized TD up to logarithmic factors. Specifically, for a $d$-dimensional value function parameter, we establish that transmitting a total of $\mathcal{O}(d \log(T))$ bits over a horizon of length $T$ suffices to achieve the order-optimal rate of $\tilde{\mathcal{O}}(1/T)$, marking an exponential improvement in communication-complexity over prior work.

items.title: The simulability frontiers of photonic quantum computing
items.summary:
Estimates of when photonic devices outgrow classical simulation are hard to compare: even for single-photon boson sampling, quoted thresholds range from 50 to 98 photons, as they rest on different tasks and assumptions. We propose as a common unit the time a classical computer needs to draw one sample from the device's exact output distribution, up to floating-point rounding. Only exactness applies equally to every kind of light, since the cost of approximate sampling depends on the accuracy required.

The simulability frontier is the device size at which our fastest exact sampler produces one sample per second on a fixed machine; this device size increases with better hardware and algorithms. As the time per sample grows exponentially with the number of detected photons, doubling the machine speed moves the frontier by about one photon, whereas a better algorithm changes the growth rate. We measure the frontier with photonic-engines, an open-source GPU library of exact samplers for single photons, entangled photons from quantum emitters, vacuum-single-photon superpositions and squeezed light.

Each sampler is validated against a simulator sharing no code with it. On one NVIDIA H100 GPU, with Haar-random interferometers, twice as many modes as photonic inputs and photon-number-resolving detectors, the frontier lies at 38.3 single photons and at 31.0 entangled photons from one emitter. For squeezed light, a timing model fitted to measurements places it at 41.5 squeezed photonic inputs of mean photon number 0.5.

For our samplers, coherence alone makes simulation harder: sources that emit a photon with probability one half reach 64.2 when vacuum and photon are mixed incoherently, as for lossy single photons, but only 50.0 when they are in coherent superposition. Feed-forward from mid-circuit measurement of up to three modes lowers the single-photon frontier only from 38.3 to 38.1.

items.title: Motivic Mirror Symmetry for Sink-recurrent Cluster Varieties
items.summary:
We prove motivic mirror symmetry for full-rank sink-recurrent cluster varieties. We allow skew-symmetrizable principal parts and invert all frozen variables.

The rational geometric motive of such a variety is isomorphic to the additive orbifold motive of the mirror stack of Hu and Shende. This gives comparisons of cohomology, higher Chow groups, and algebraic $K$-theory with rational coefficients.

The proof combines quantum deformation with the splitting of these motives into Tate summands. For really full-rank skew-symmetric seeds, a finite étale morphism realizes the comparison.

We also study this geometric comparison in families over the projective line.

items.title: On $\mathrm{HH}^1$ of blocks of finite simple group algebras
items.summary:
Let $G$ be a sporadic simple group, $k$ a field of positive characteristic and assume $B$ is a block of $kG$ with non-trivial defect.

In this paper we prove the first Hochschild cohomology group $\mathrm{HH}^1(B)$ is non-vanishing.

Furthermore, we prove that for every wild block with abelian defect of a sporadic simple group, we have that $\mathrm{HH}^1(B)$ is a solvable Lie algebra of derived length two, with non-zero maximal toral rank.

items.title: GARI++: A General-Purpose Decoder for Quantum Error Correction
items.summary:
We present GARI++, a two-stage decoding pipeline achieving accuracy competitive with the state of the art across surface, bivariate bicycle and color codes without relying on ensembles. The first stage uses GARI, a normalized min-sum decoder with random serial scheduling on the GARI transformed matrix.

The second stage decoder is used only for the cases that the first stage does not converge, and the decoder is configurable based on the choice of the QEC code. The first stage pipelines towards the second stage both the residual syndrome and the soft information.

GARI++ pipelining is predictive, meaning that GARI++ chooses the first stage iteration outputs which are expected to deliver the best accuracy in the second stage. GARI++ motivates a hybrid FPGA-CPU architecture for real-time decoding.

For example, under uniform circuit-level depolarising noise with a physical error rate of 0.001, the FPGA implementation of GARI achieves average latencies per round ranging from $201 ns$ to $11.8μs$ for surface code distances between 7 and 25. At the same time, due to the very low weight residuals output by the first stage, the average residual decoding time per round remains near constant and below one microsecond on a single Apple M2 core for surface code distances even up to 51 when using Union-Find and accuracy on par with correlated MWPM.

items.title: A short proof of the Aaronson-Ambainis Conjecture via the completion framework
items.summary:
We give a short proof of the Aaronson-Ambainis conjecture.

If a partial Boolean function $f$ is defined on a $δ$-fraction of all $n$-bit strings and have quantum query complexity $Q(f)$, then, for every $0<ε<1$, a deterministic algorithm computes $f$ correctly on at least a $1-ε$ fraction of its domain using $O( Q(f)^6 / (εδ)^2)$ queries.

Our proof uses the completion framework and establishes a more general bound in terms of the classical adversary measure.

The only result we use from Turturean's recent proof is a special case of his certificate inequality, for which we provide a self-contained proof.

We also derive the stronger variant of the Aaronson-Ambainis Conjecture, the bounded-polynomial influence conjecture, from our main result in the appendix.

items.title: Strong pseudo Frobenius numbers
items.summary:
By Sylow's theorem, the number of Sylow $p$-subgroups of a finite group is congruent to $1$ modulo $p$, but not every such integer occurs. Frobenius extended the congruence to the number of subgroups of order $p^a$ for every $a\ge0$.

Kulakoff and Hall showed that this number is congruent to $1$ or $1+p$ modulo $p^2$ whenever $p^{a+1}$ divides the group order. A positive integer is a Frobenius $p$-number if it is the number of subgroups of order $p^a$ of some finite group for some $a$.

There are integers congruent to $1$ modulo $p^2$ which are not Frobenius $p$-numbers, and it remained open whether there are also such integers congruent to $1+p$ modulo $p^2$. We show that no finite group has exactly $106$ subgroups of order $5^a$ for any $a\ge0$.

items.title: Quantum Simulation of Quantum Channels and Applications
items.summary:
We review the basic theory of quantum channels and develop a strategy for simulating them on digital quantum computers, drawing upon the \emph{Choi-Kraus operator-sum representation} and Stinespring dilation to provide a unified approach for various applications. We discuss three types of applications, offering explicit examples for each: the preparation of mixed states, measurements described by positive operator-valued measures (POVMs), and the simulation of the evolution of Markovian quantum systems.

We recover fundamental concepts from quantum theory, such as the purification of a mixed state and the Naimark dilation associated with a POVM. Regarding the simulation of the evolution of a Markovian quantum system, we introduce an operator, termed the residual operator, to construct, from the system's Liouvillian, a quantum channel that serves as a first-order approximation of the quantum dynamical semigroup.

This allows the simulation of quantum dynamics to be performed in a manner analogous to the Euler method for ordinary differential equations, avoiding Trotterization. We prove all the theoretical results mentioned, with the exception of the fundamental Choi-Kraus theorem concerning the operator-sum representation of quantum channels, for which we provide the appropriate references.

The explicit simulations discussed were implemented using the AerSimulator from IBM's Qiskit SDK, with the corresponding code available on GitHub.

items.title: Unified architecture for arbitrary two-qubit gates with neutral atoms
items.summary:
We propose a unified architecture for two-qubit gates in neutral-atom quantum processors which allows the implementation of the complete set of two-qubit gates.

Our approach rests on a single resource that unlocks the entire gate set: an XXZ interaction with tunable anisotropy, combined only with single-qubit operations.

We introduce a Rydberg-atom realization of the tunable XXZ interaction and combine it with optimally controlled global microwave pulses to implement the B, QFT, iSWAP, and $\sqrt{\mathrm{iSWAP}}$ gates, as well as a continuous gate family interpolating from CZ to iSWAP via the B gate.

This work allows the implementation of any two-qubit gate natively in neutral-atom platforms, enabling flexible switching between instruction sets to reduce circuit depth and compilation overhead in quantum algorithm implementation.

items.title: An efficient classical algorithm for OTOCs in chaotic quantum dynamics
items.summary:
Estimating out-of-time-ordered correlators (OTOCs) in individual instances of random quantum circuits has been proposed as a candidate for verifiable quantum advantage, and demonstrated to be hard for conventional classical algorithms such as tensor networks and Monte Carlo. Using insights from quantum chaos, we develop and implement a polynomial-time classical algorithm for the four-point ${\rm OTOC}^{(1)}$ and the eight-point ${\rm OTOC}^{(2)}$ in typical instances of one-dimensional (1D) quantum circuits.

Our results demonstrate average-case classical tractability of estimating OTOCs in the sensitive regime where circuit-to-circuit fluctuations are large. Our algorithm organizes the OTOC into a rapidly converging series, where the leading term includes contributions from histories within permutation degrees of freedom in the replicated Hilbert space, and subleading terms arise from excursions outside this space.

Although chaos is often viewed as an insurmountable barrier to classical simulation, our algorithm exploits a form of dephasing caused by chaos, which suppresses the subleading terms. We provide strong theoretical and numerical evidence to support this suppression.

Further, we demonstrate that practical implementations of our algorithm estimate ${\rm OTOC}^{(1)}$ and ${\rm OTOC}^{(2)}$ in 1D circuits with high accuracy, achieving higher signal-to-noise ratio at larger circuit depths compared to recent 2D experiments by Google. Extending our algorithm to higher dimensions, and resolving the status of quantum advantage in 2D OTOCs, remain open problems.

items.title: IonQ and Carahsoft Partner to Bring Quantum Solutions to the Public Sector
items.summary:
Insider Brief

IonQ and Carahsoft have formed a strategic partnership to expand U.S. public sector access to quantum computing, networking, sensing and security technologies.

Carahsoft will serve as IonQ ‘s public sector distributor, supporting procurement, contract access and sales through its reseller network and Federal systems integrators.

The partnership builds on IonQ ‘s existing government work, including its progression to Stage C of DARPA’s Quantum Benchmarking Initiative and its quantum networking collaboration with the Air Force Research Laboratory.

PRESS RELEASE — IonQ (NYSE: IONQ ), a leading full-stack quantum platform and foundry, and Carahsoft Technology Corp. , The Trusted Government IT Solutions Provider ® , today announced a strategic partnership. The collaboration intends to drive quantum computing, networking, sensing and security adoption across Federal agencies and their industry partners. Under the agreement, Carahsoft will serve as IonQ’s Public Sector distributor, enabling Government agencies to purchase IonQ technology through its reseller partners.

The IonQ -Carahsoft partnership comes as the Federal Government accelerates its commitment to quantum innovation. Executive Order 14413, Ushering in the Next Frontier of Quantum Innovation , directs a Government-wide strategy to advance quantum commercialization, deployment and collaboration with U.S. industry. Through this partnership, IonQ and Carahsoft aim to expand Federal access to emerging quantum technologies, streamline procurement and support mission-critical national security objectives.

“ IonQ and Carahsoft will have a powerful partnership across the entire Public Sector, including higher education, State, Local Government, Department of War, civilian and the integrator and partner community,” said Steve Harris, IonQ Senior Vice President and General Manager, Public Sector. “Through this relationship quantum solutions ranging from computing, networking, security to sensing will be more readily accessible during this important time when quantum progress is an immediate and critical requirement.”

items.title: Sequential vs parallel Strategies for Sharing Quantum Advantage in Communication Tasks
items.summary:
Information can be extracted from a quantum system in a sustainable manner, allowing the system to be reused for further information extraction through subsequent interactions. We investigate the possibility of consensus between two experimentally feasible methods, namely, parallel and sequential sharing, that enable multiple observers to extract information encoded in a quantum system.

We show that any statistics generated by a parallel sharing strategy can be reproduced by a sequential strategy when only two observers are involved. However, when more than two observers participate in sharing quantum correlations, certain statistics achievable through parallel strategies cannot be reproduced by sequential strategies.

Moreover, we demonstrate that sharing quantum advantage through a parallel strategy is impossible for a class of communication tasks involving two decoding measurements, thereby establishing an arbitrarily large gap between the sustainability of quantum advantage under sequential and parallel strategies. This naturally raises the question of whether this impossibility extends to communication tasks involving more than two decoding measurements.

We show that, while parallel sharing of quantum advantage is impossible in a 3-bit random access code (RAC), it becomes possible in a 3-bit parity-oblivious RAC, where at most two observers can simultaneously obtain a quantum advantage by performing measurements on two imperfect clones of the initially prepared quantum system. Our findings have potential applications in the development of quantum communication networks and distributed quantum information processing.

items.title: Semiampleness of Hodge line bundles and b-semiampleness of the moduli part
items.summary:
We give proofs of Hodge semiampleness and b-semiampleness without using o-minimality. We establish a geometric semiampleness criterion for line bundles on proper algebraic spaces. Let $(X,D)$ be a log smooth pair with $X$ a proper algebraic space.

For an integral polarizable pure variation of Calabi--Yau type on $X\setminus D$ with unipotent local monodromy, let $L$ be its extended highest Hodge line. If $L$ is numerically integrable and has torsion combinatorial monodromy, then $L$ is semiample. We also prove semiampleness of extended Griffiths lines.

We construct normal projective period compactifications on which a positive power of the Griffiths line extends to an ample line bundle. As an application, we prove that the moduli b-divisor $\mathbf{M}$ of a projective lc-trivial fibration over a normal algebraic variety is b-semiample, provided that the generic boundary is effective. Suppose further that the geometric generic pair is klt and its boundary is big, with nonzero coefficients in a fixed finite set $I\subset(0,1)\cap\mathbb{Q}$.

Then $c\mathbf{M}$ is b-Cartier and b-free for an integer $c>0$ depending only on the relative dimension and $I$. We extend b-semiampleness to analogous projective fibrations over normal complex analytic bases, assuming a global relative polarization and an invertible log pluricanonical sheaf pulled back from the base.

items.title: Inference Validation for Regulated AI: Building a Decision Pipeline on NVIDIA AIPerf
items.summary:
Deploying large language models in regulated industries requires more than picking the fastest inference engine: it requires evidence that a configuration meets contractual and legal obligations before it serves a single customer request.

We describe Runway, an internal validation harness built at MasterControl that builds a governed decision pipeline around NVIDIA AIPerf.

The key insight is separating concerns: AIPerf provides the trusted measurement, while Runway provides the experiment design that comes before it and the compliance, cost, and audit decisions that come after.

We describe the architecture and the storage model that makes caching and audit one mechanism.

We report three findings from Runway sweeps: TensorRT-LLM and vLLM rankings invert with concurrency; a newer, pricier GPU instance can be the cheaper one per request; and speculative decoding behaves differently across engines under load, so engine configuration can outweigh engine choice.

items.title: Spin Shuttling Through Quantum-Dot Based Chiral Molecular Bridges: Gauge Constraints, Holonomy, and Quantum Gates
items.summary:
Chiral molecular bridges between silicon quantum dots can provide novel two-qubit entangling resources via the chirality-induced spin-selectivity (CISS) effect. We evaluate this using Makhlin invariants.

Modeling a phase-coherent bridge as an $\mathrm{SU}(2)$-valued hopping between two spins, a Schrieffer-Wolff reduction yields a twisted exchange interaction $J \mathbf{S}_1 \cdot \mathbf{R} \mathbf{S}_2$, whose Dzyaloshinskii-Moriya and symmetric anisotropic parts are fixed by a single bridge angle $α$. Using the Kaplan-Shekhtman-Entin-Wohlman-Aharony (KSEA) gauge argument, we prove this interaction is locally equivalent to isotropic exchange; thus, a single chiral bond does not constitute a new entangling class.

Breaking this gauge symmetry reveals genuine chiral utility: chiral exchange converts a uniform transverse field into a synthetic gradient, bringing the two-qubit propagator within $7\times10^{-4}$ of the CNOT class in invariant space 4.7 times faster than an equivalent orthogonal gradient. Shuttling a spin through bridges with non-collinear axes implements a non-Abelian $\mathrm{SU}(2)$ holonomy, yielding rotationally non-reciprocal transport and closed-loop geometric gates that suppress dynamical-phase noise to second order.

To address the unsettled microscopic origin of CISS, we introduce a unified transport channel combining coherent rotation, a direction-reversing spin filter, and pointer-basis dephasing. This model obeys an exact $\tanh$ composition law for pumped polarization and a closed-form transverse decay law, yielding four observables that experimentally over-determine the bridge's coherent fraction $F_c$.

Finally, we quantify silicon-specific hardware constraints, establishing the Landau-Zener valley-adiabaticity window ($E_v \geq 2.1\sqrt{\hbar v}$) and charge-noise limit ($σ_J/J \leq 3\%$) required for $99\%$ gate fidelity.

items.title: No Exponential Quantum Advantage for Decoded Quantum Interferometry with Local Quantum Decoders
items.summary:
Decoded quantum interferometry (DQI) reduces optimization of sparse linear constraint problems, and sampling from their Gibbs measures, to decoding a linear code from a quantum state. We study DQI on random $D$-regular $k$-sparse instances with $k\ge3$, for which local decoders such as belief propagation with quantum messages (BPQM) are commonly used. Such decoders estimate a typical codeword symbol using only the qudits within logarithmic distance of it.

Our main insight is that the thresholds of the decoding problem induced by DQI correspond to phase transitions of the Gibbs measure that are well studied in statistical physics: tree reconstruction for local decoders and, for Max-$k$-XORSAT, condensation for the optimal decoder. This insight allows us to prove two main results. First, we prove an information-theoretic obstruction: no local decoder can recover the codeword with high probability above the tree reconstruction threshold.

Conversely, we show that a decoder based on BPQM reaches this threshold. Since the cavity method predicts that local Markov chains equilibrate rapidly up to the same threshold, we expect DQI with local decoders to give no exponential speedup for sampling and no advantage in approximate optimization with amplitude functions that depend only on the number of violated constraints. Second, we consider the optimal decoder (the pretty-good measurement, for which no efficient implementation is known) and show that it succeeds exactly below the condensation threshold.

The condensation threshold thus provides a tight upper bound on the performance of DQI with these amplitude functions, providing a strict refinement of the limit that Jordan et al.\ derived from the Holevo bound. Our results point to efficient nonlocal decoders that succeed between the two thresholds as the only viable path to a quantum advantage with DQI on these instances.

items.title: Polynomial-Space Quantum Algorithms from Classical Branching: Colouring, Domination and Monotone Local Search
items.summary:
We give quantum algorithms for exponential-time problems on $n$ vertices or elements, with bounded error, polynomial space and no quantum random access memory. Our results are these.

(1) 4-Colouring in quantum time $O(1.3032^n)$, from a polynomial-space branching algorithm with polynomial-space terminal algorithms; with the branching algorithm alone, $O(1.3100^n)$. The previous best bound in this model, to our knowledge, is $O(1.3231^n)$.

(2) $k$-Colouring below the previous best bound for $k \in \{5, 7, 8, 9, 10, 11\}$ and $13 \le k \le 18$, from $O(1.4518^n)$ for $k = 5$ to $O(1.9233^n)$ for $k = 18$. (3) Dominating Set in $O(1.2235^n)$, against the previous $O(2^{n/2})$, Independent Dominating Set in $O(1.1583^n)$, and Edge Dominating Set and Minimum Maximal Matching in $O(1.1501^n)$.

(4) A quantum form of monotone local search: if the extension problem has a backtracking tree with $c^k$ nodes up to polynomial factors, the problem is solved in quantum time $(2 - 1/c)^{n/2}$ up to polynomial factors. This gives Feedback Vertex Set in $O(1.3081^n)$, Subset and Group Feedback Vertex Set in $O(1.3229^n)$, Cluster Vertex Deletion in $O(1.2033^n)$, 3-Hitting Set in $O(1.2405^n)$, Proper Interval Vertex Deletion in $O(1.3541^n)$, Multicut on Trees in $O(1.1647^n)$ and Min-Ones $d$-SAT in $O^*((2-1/d)^{n/2})$.

(5) Quantum exponential-time approximations below the quantum exact bounds, such as a 1.1-approximation for Vertex Cover in $O(1.0555^n)$ and for Feedback Vertex Set in $O(1.2161^n)$. The colouring exponents for $k \ge 6$ come from an evaluation of a known reduction recursion, computed in floating point with a margin.

items.title: A local language model layered with rule-based and neural detectors for clinical text de-identification: an open-source toolkit and evaluation
items.summary:
Objectives: To measure whether a locally hosted large language model (LLM), stacked with deterministic and clinical named-entity recognition (NER) detectors, finds more protected health information (PHI) than open tools, and at what precision.

Materials and Methods: DeidSharp, an open-source .NET toolkit, combines the findings of pluggable detectors (patterns, a clinical NER model, a local 26B mixture-of-experts LLM) and fails closed on any detector error. Configurations fixed on tuning halves were compared, under a prespecified protocol, with deid, Philter, the Stanford/Penn de-identifier, OpenAI Privacy Filter and GLiNER on reporting halves of PhysioNet's nursing notes (889 spans) and semi-synthetic MIMIC-IV-Note discharge summaries (29,023 spans), and on synthetic ASQ-PHI queries, with paired patient-level bootstrap intervals.

Results: In the nursing notes, against Stanford/Penn, the recall-first stack found 98.9% of PHI (+2.8, 95% CI 1.4 to 4.4) at 9.3 points lower precision; the precision-first stack, without NER, found 96.5%, matching Stanford/Penn, at 19.6 points higher precision (83.2%). In the discharge summaries, both stacks led Stanford/Penn by more than 20 points (recall-first 95.3%, +21.5, 20.5 to 22.4), almost entirely on generated untyped names; on typed labels all three exceeded 99%. All four prespecified comparisons held. No configuration beat deid significantly on its home corpus; Philter found more discharge-summary spans than the recall-first stack at 23 points lower precision.

Discussion: The LLM was the main detector and NER added place names; asked to verify its own findings, the LLM discarded a quarter of true PHI.

Conclusion: A local LLM layered with deterministic detectors offers recall-first and precision-first operating points without sending text off-site.

items.title: Quantum Residual Exploration for Selected Configuration Interaction
items.summary:
We propose a modular hybrid quantum-classical method to improve selected configuration interaction at a fixed final determinant budget.

Quantum measurements supply complementary determinants, accepted only when they outrank classical candidates under a common energetic criterion.

This targets multistep excitations that perturbative discovery may miss in strongly correlated systems.

A demonstration on the Quantinuum Reimei trapped-ion quantum computer shows that measured proposals for H$_{12}$ at a stretched geometry lower the variational energy relative to classical-only selection at the same final determinant budget.

items.title: How Far Does Second-Order Linear Response Predict Quantization Mismatch? Pre-Registered Measurements on Five Language Models
items.summary:
Serving systems choose a weight format for each model and deployment. A low-cost screen predicts the resulting KL divergence from the unquantized model's Fisher information using $\tfrac12Δ^\top FΔ$, the expansion underlying Hessian-aware and second-order post-training quantizers. We assess the reliability of this screen in GPU batches with channel-wise int8, per-tensor fp8 and group-wise int4 on Qwen3-8B, Qwen3-4B, OLMo-2-7B, Qwen3-32B and Qwen3-30B-A3B.

Relative predictions hold across a 16-fold range of perturbation scales, int4 group sizes and rounding modes, while absolute predictions are heavy-tailed. A trimmed average brings 10 of 12 cells on Qwen3-4B and OLMo-2 within 15% of measured KL. The MoE model exhibits nonquadratic response at small perturbations, with int8 KL scaling as $α^{0.63}$.

Computing per-sequence gradients in bf16 can cause fourfold prediction errors. We trace these errors to arithmetic in the lower half of the backward pass and eliminate them by using fp32 there. Batch-invariant kernels run at 0.55 times the throughput, while changes in reduction order introduce a floor of 0.17-0.22 nats per sequence.

We build a screener with one streamed fp32 Fisher pass, trimmed tensor-block predictions with a band, a flag for aligned tensors and per-layer format allocation. On the unseen Mistral-7B-v0.3 family, all six predictions fall within the band, all three KL budgets are met, and vLLM throughput is predicted within 0.4%.

items.title: On the Cohomological Amplitude of the Locally Analytic Jacquet--Langlands Functor
items.summary:
We prove a local cohomological bound $RΓ_{\mathrm{pro\acute et}}(X,\mathcal F)\in D^{[0,\dim X]}$ for a pro-étale sheaf with a derived $p$-complete integral lattice whose modulo $p^m$ reductions are filtered colimits of finite local systems on an affinoid topologically of finite type over $C$.

For $G=\mathrm{GL}_n(F)$, with $n\geq2$ and $F/\mathbb Q_p$ finite, we apply these local bounds to variants of Scholze's Jacquet--Langlands functor $\mathrm{JL}_\mathscr{B}(Π):= RΓ_{\mathrm{pro\acute et}}(\mathbb{P}^{n-1}_C,\mathcal{F}_Π\otimes^{L, \square}_{\mathbb{Q}_p}\mathscr{B})$ for $\mathscr{B}\in\{\mathbb{Q}_p, \widehat{\mathscr{O}}, \mathbb{B}_J\}$ and Banach or compact-type LB representations $Π$ of $G$, obtaining $\mathrm{JL}_{\mathscr{B}}(Π)\in D^{[0,2(n-1)]}$ for each choice of $\mathscr{B}$.

We also prove that for arbitrary continuous principal series $I(η)=(\mathrm{Ind}_B^Gη)^{\mathrm{cont}}$, we have $\mathrm{JL}(\mathrm{Ind}_B^Gη)\in D^{[0, n]}$, while $\mathrm{JL}_{\widehat{\mathscr{O}}}(I(η)),\mathrm{JL}_{\mathbb{B}_J}(I(η))\in D^{[0, n-1]}$.

items.title: hzero Emerges From Stealth to Coordinate Quantum and Classical Computing
items.summary:
Insider Brief

hzero has emerged from stealth to develop software that coordinates workloads and resources across quantum and classical computing systems.

The software is designed to integrate with existing computing tools and adjust resource use based on application requirements, operating conditions and operator priorities.

Led by co-founders Bruno G. Taketani and Martin Rüfenacht, the company is backed by LEA Ventures, FORWARD.one and Leo Capital.

hzero has emerged from stealth with software designed to help quantum computers and classical computing systems work together, backed by investors including LEA Ventures, FORWARD.one and Leo Capital.

The Munich, Germany-based company is developing a software layer that coordinates computing jobs and resources across quantum processors and high-performance computing infrastructure. Its approach is designed to work with the scheduling tools, application software and quantum computing systems that operators already use.

Co-founders Bruno G. Taketani, chief executive, and Martin Rüfenacht, chief technology officer, lead the company. The team brings experience in quantum hardware, control systems, high-performance computing and systems software, according to the company’s website.

items.title: All-to-all connectivity via adiabatic ZZ interactions in a superconducting flux qubit processor
items.summary:
Scalable superconducting quantum processors would benefit from high qubit connectivity, yet existing architectures connect neighbouring qubits via tunable couplers, which introduce substantial wiring and control overhead. Here, we propose a baseband-driven adiabatic ZZ gate that entangles any selected pair in a register of flux qubits coupled via a common cavity.

The qubits stay dc-biased at their flux sweet spot. Strong drives applied selectively through local flux lines, at frequencies far below the qubit transitions, adiabatically tilt the quantization axes and generate an effective longitudinal ZZ interaction.

The strength of the coupling is tunable and controlled by the amplitudes and relative phase of the drives rather than by any resonance condition. Numerical simulations give coherent gate errors below $10^{-4}$ over broad ranges of drive frequency, with comparable fidelities for two simultaneous gates in a four-qubit register.

The protocol is robust against frequency fluctuations and remains effective even when many qubits are coupled to the cavity.

items.title: Lie algebras graded by the root system $AG_2$
items.summary:
We study Lie algebras graded by the generalized root system $AG_2$, which is obtained from $G_2$ by adjoining the doubles of its short roots, over fields of characteristic different from $2$ and $3$. We show that every such Lie algebra with a grading subalgebra of type $A_2$ is, modulo its center, the Tits-Kantor-Koecher Lie algebra of a structurable algebra equipped with an idempotent $t$ satisfying $t+\overline{t}=1$.

Conversely, every structurable algebra with such an idempotent gives rise to an $(AG_2,A_2)$-graded Lie algebra. We describe the corresponding Peirce decomposition and characterize the additional algebraic structure required for an $(AG_2,G_2)$-grading.

Using the classification of central simple structurable algebras, we determine the central simple examples when the characteristic is also different from $5$. Finally, we compare our constructions with the theory of Tits hexagons.

For the central simple examples in which all root spaces are non-zero, we determine which ones are Tits-hexagonalizable; in certain cases, this imposes an additional balancing condition on the idempotent.

items.title: EV Group Helps Accelerate Qubit Scaling for Quantum Computing Through Advanced Packaging Expertise
items.summary:
Insider Brief

EV Group (EVG) is applying its semiconductor manufacturing expertise in advanced packaging, heterogeneous integration and photonics to help quantum chip developers address manufacturing challenges as they scale quantum computing systems.

Its process technologies include fusion and hybrid bonding, oxide-free bonding, digital and nanoimprint lithography, and thin-wafer processing, which support different quantum hardware architectures.

EVG’s quantum computing activities include collaborations with Xanadu and Silicon Austria Labs, including the CHAMP-ION pilot line project for industrial-scale production of ion-trap quantum chips.

PRESS RELEASE — EV Group (EVG), a leading provider of innovative process solutions and expertise serving leading-edge and future semiconductor designs and chip integration schemes, today announced that it is supporting quantum chip developers and manufacturers in addressing the complex manufacturing requirements associated with scaling quantum computing systems. Building on its ongoing contributions to quantum chip development, EVG is applying its established expertise in advanced packaging, heterogeneous integration and photonics manufacturing to help customers develop and validate new product designs and manufacturing processes for increasingly complex quantum architectures.

EVG will highlight its suite of process solutions for quantum computing and other critical technologies at SEMICON Europa, the premier microelectronics and semiconductor manufacturing supply chain event in Europe, taking place this week on November 10-13 at the Messe München in Munich, Germany.

New Manufacturing Approaches Need to Scale Quantum Computing

items.title: Semisimple Deformations of Contraction Algebras for Smooth Threefold Flops
items.summary:
Building on Bryan--Katz--Leung, Hua--Toda and Kawamata, we study deformations of contraction algebras and the local geometry of the scheme of associative algebra laws. Let $A$ be the basic contraction algebra of a completed projective flopping contraction of a smooth complex threefold. We construct a finite free polynomial family that is constant and semisimple away from the origin, with the original curve projectors fixed.

For each restricted positive root $β=(β_i)$, with coordinates indexed by the retained vertices, the split generic fibre has $n_β$ matrix blocks of size $\sum_iβ_i$, and the labelled projector $e_i$ has rank $β_i$ on each block. Here $n_β$ is the corresponding genus-zero Gopakumar--Vafa invariant. If the geometric generic fibre of a finite free associative formal deformation of $A$ is semisimple, it has the same matrix factors, and any lifts of the original projectors have the same ranks on those factors.

The scheme of associative algebra laws is smooth at $A$. The closure of the corresponding semisimple orbit is its unique irreducible component through $A$. The proof uses the curve divisors of Katz--Morrison and Nabijou--Wemyss, presentations of the universal contraction quotient and its cocenter, and the orbit method of Jelisiejew--Smoktunowicz.

These presentations prove the geometric Hua--Toda flatness assertions. In the geometric families considered here, the relative contraction algebra, its centre and its cocenter are finite free over arbitrary complete Noetherian local complex bases. On a smooth open neighbourhood of $A$ in the scheme of algebra laws, the centres and cocenters form dual vector bundles compatible with arbitrary base change.

For the type $D$ algebras $D_{n,2}$ with $n\ge2$, the centre morphism gives counterexamples to the smoothness assertion in Conjecture 1.4(2) of Jelisiejew--Smoktunowicz.

items.title: Horizon Quantum Integrates OQC’s 32-Qubit Processor with Triple Alpha
items.summary:
Insider Brief

Horizon Quantum and OQC have integrated OQC’s 32-qubit superconducting quantum processor, Toshiko, with Horizon Quantum’s Triple Alpha development environment to enable pulse-level hardware control.

The integration allows developers to characterise qubits, measure coherence parameters such as T1 and T2, and perform quantum gate calibration within the same environment used to develop quantum applications.

The collaboration aims to simplify hardware characterisation and calibration workflows by giving developers access to pulse-level control through Triple Alpha’s programming environment and web-based API.

PRESS RELEASE — Horizon Quantum Computing Pte. Ltd., the wholly-owned subsidiary of Horizon Quantum Holdings Ltd. (Nasdaq: HQ) (“Horizon Quantum”), a pioneer of software infrastructure for quantum applications, and OQC, a global leader in quantum computing, today announced the successful pulse-level integration of OQC’s QPU with Triple Alpha, Horizon Quantum’s integrated development environment, as part of an ongoing collaboration.

This integration provides access to the hardware control layer, enabling Triple Alpha users to perform pulse-level operations on the OQC’s 32-qubit device Toshiko, allowing them to build hardware characterization and gate calibration procedures within the same environment they use to develop and execute quantum applications.

Characterization is a key step in preparing quantum hardware for practical use. By measuring the physical properties of QPUs, characterization helps build an understanding of processor behavior and informs the calibration of quantum gates, ultimately improving computational fidelity. QPUs need a universal gate set to execute quantum programs, and each gate must be calibrated. This process involves sending pulses to the processor, measuring qubit responses, and adjusting the pulses to achieve the desired operations. Because quantum systems are highly sensitive, frequent recalibration is necessary.

items.title: Universal two-qubit control across dilution refrigerators via a 10-km coherent optical link
items.summary:
Distributed quantum networks are important for scalable quantum processors and for potential applications in communication, distributed computation, and sensing, in which direct classical links for adaptive control are essential to harness the shared entanglement. However, controlling superconducting quantum processors from a separate refrigerator over long distances remains elusive.

Here, we introduce a coherent optical link (COL) that delivers microwave waveforms and their phase references between dilution refrigerators. Combining a laser, a microwave-to-optical transducer and an optical-to-microwave photodiode, the COL transmits microwave control signals over 10~km of fiber, while optical references derived from the same laser compensate for the frequency mismatch between devices.

Through the COL, we deliver a universal gate set to a transmon qubit and a cavity qubit in another refrigerator and entangle them, and achieve a Bell-state fidelity of 80.6\%. Quantum control delivered through the COL thus provides a classical backbone for modular quantum processors.

items.title: Phrase-Level Speculative Decoding on a Frozen Target
items.summary:
Speculative decoders raise throughput by banking more target tokens per forward pass, and Medusa, EAGLE-3, DFlash and DSpark all do it the same way: more candidates that survive verification. All of them draft in the target's own vocabulary, so one node of the candidate tree is one target token, and the tokenizer makes that unit look like a constant.

It is not. BPE's pretokenizer splits on whitespace before merges are learned, so no multi-word string can ever become a single token: in Qwen3-4B, "United States of America" is four tokens and no adjacent pair of them exists as one entry, so a phrase is out of reach of any method drafting in the target's vocabulary.

We change the unit. A small MLP head reads the frozen target's hidden state and predicts a one- to three-word phrase as one entry in a separate draft vocabulary; greedy longest-match expansion maps it back into the target's own tokens, and N candidates are verified in one forward pass behind a prefix-tree mask, so the change is orthogonal to tree depth and width.

The target and its tokenizer stay frozen and a candidate is accepted only while it matches the target's own argmax, so the served output is identical to greedy decoding up to floating-point tie-breaking. On one A5000 at batch 1, against HuggingFace generate(), a 21.94M head (0.545% of Qwen3-4B) reaches 2.391x on GSM8K, 2.444x on MATH-500 and 1.544x on MT-Bench.

Because the head's output layer is one row of 257 parameters per entry, the draft vocabulary size is the parameter budget: an 8,000-entry head is 3.434M parameters, 0.0854% of the target and 64x smaller than EAGLE-3's drafter, and keeps 92.3% of the larger head's GSM8K tokens per pass. With EAGLE-3 run on same prompts and baseline, our 21.94M head is ahead of tree-16 on both maths sets and behind tree-60 on every set.

items.title: Gorenstein modules over Thompson's group
items.summary:
Let $k$ be any commutative ring of characteristic $0$.

We construct an example of a countably presented Gorenstein projective module over the algebra of Thompson's group $F$ with coefficients in $k$, that is not Benson cofibrant.

In particular, we provide a negative answer to a conjecture proposed by Dembegioti and Talelli.

The construction uses a general method that produces totally acyclic complexes of flat modules and is based on the computation of the (co-)cohomology of $F$ by Brown and Geoghegan.

items.title: DForkTree: Accelerating Speculative Decoding with Fork-Aware Block Diffusion Draft Trees
items.summary:
Speculative decoding speeds up language models by letting a lightweight drafter propose several future tokens that the target model verifies in parallel. Block diffusion drafters such as DFlash draft a whole block in one forward pass, and DDTree builds a draft tree from their per-position distributions.

Each of these distributions assumes that the drafter's own most likely continuation is correct. A tree, however, gains over a chain only on branches that leave this continuation, where the drafter's top-1 accuracy drops from 89% to 18% and its candidate lists miss the right token far more often.

When re-run from the fork token, the same drafter is usually correct, so the errors come from the prefix that the distributions condition on rather than from what the drafter knows. We introduce DForkTree, a training-free method that re-anchors each branch on its own tokens.

DForkTree adds n-gram statistics from the target model's own outputs to the drafter's scores as pointwise mutual information, weights them more after the fork, and builds the optimal tree under these scores exactly on the GPU. On Qwen3.5-4B and 9B, with all tree methods sharing one drafter, tree pipeline and verifier, DForkTree is the fastest tree method on every benchmark.

It is up to 41.5% faster than DFlash and 15.1% faster than DDTree in the same setting, with average speedups of up to 4.75x over autoregressive decoding.

items.title: Split Kernel Multiplication Modules
items.summary:
We introduce split kernel multiplication (SKM) modules, for which every submodule has the form $N=IM\oplus\ker f$, where $I$ is an ideal of $R$ and $f$ is an endomorphism of $M$. We study direct sums, localization, and connections with multiplication and retractability properties.

For the idempotent version (ISKM), we prove that $R\oplus k^b$ is ISKM over a local ring $(R,\mathfrak m)$, with residue field $k$ and $b\geq1$, if and only if $\mathfrak m^2=0$. We also classify ISKM modules of the form $R^a\oplus k^b$ over local rings.

For commutative Noetherian rings, we show that $R^2$ is SKM if and only if $R$ is an Artinian principal ideal ring. Finally, we prove that every finitely generated $R$-module is ISKM if and only if $R$ is a finite product of fields.

items.title: Calibration-free quantum thermometry with strain-swept two-level defects
items.summary:
Superconducting qubits operate within a well-defined temperature range, making local temperature monitoring important. Here we show that intrinsic two-level defects in Josephson-junction barriers can act as local thermometers by exploiting the shape of their population response, without requiring calibration of the readout offset or contrast.

Marginalizing over these unknown parameters imposes an identifiability requirement absent from single-parameter thermometric bounds: for narrow sweeps, usable information scales as the fourth power of the sweep width. Hence, a narrow sweep becomes locally indistinguishable from a change in offset or contrast.

We illustrate this principle with a strain-swept two-level defect in a Josephson junction. For a reported defect with tunneling energy $Δ_{0}/h=\SI{1.3}{\giga\hertz}$, swept along one branch of its hyperbola to \SI{2.69}{\giga\hertz} (an asymmetry excursion of \SI{2.36}{\giga\hertz}, or \SI{8}{\volt} of piezo voltage), the analysis projects a single-defect fit precision of \SI{0.58}{\percent} at \SI{20}{\milli\kelvin}.

The resulting response enables temperature estimation without prior calibration of the readout offset and contrast, while the same sweep overdetermines the Boltzmann form and identifies significant deviations from thermality. These results establish intrinsic junction defects as a resource for calibration-free local thermometry and highlight identifiability as a key design criterion for primary temperature sensing.

items.title: Prune, Don't Merge: Expert Compression of Mixture-of-Experts LLMs on Multilingual Production Tasks
items.summary:
Mixture-of-Experts language models are cheap to run per token but expensive to hold in GPU memory, which drives the cost of serving them in production. One-shot expert compression shrinks them after a single calibration pass.

Its two current state-of-the-art methods are REAP for expert pruning, which deletes the least salient experts, and REAM for expert merging, which merges them into the most salient ones. Both have been evaluated only on academic benchmarks.

We compare the two on five multilingual production tasks of a web-hosting company, from classification to the generation of marketing HTML email templates, with two 30B-parameter models (Qwen3-30B-A3B-Instruct-2507 and the hybrid Mamba-attention Nemotron-3.5-Lightning) at 25% and 50% of experts removed and the same calibration data. Pruning wins: on the same rows, REAP is significantly better in 16 of 20 comparisons and REAM in 2.

At 25%, REAP keeps 93.6% of Qwen3-30B's generative quality and REAM 62.5%, although on benchmarks the two are within a point for the same model. The damage concentrates in the output contract rather than the content: 89.8-95.2% of each significant loss on email templates comes from hard-gate failures such as invalid JSON, broken mobile layouts and runaway generation, and most failed non-English domain descriptions copy the prompt's English opening phrase.

Cross-perplexity and logit divergence, two diagnostics from the REAP paper, also track production quality, as does the rate of repetition loops; n-gram diversity does not. We close with practical guidance for compressing MoE models for production.

items.title: Commuting-check gauging for fault-tolerant logical measurements
items.summary:
Gauging turns a logical operator into a product of local checks, providing a route to logical measurement and lattice surgery. These checks can fail to commute outside the code space, so measuring one can randomize the outcome of another.

In this work, we introduce completion qubits that make the checks commute for Clifford $\mathbb{Z}_2$ symmetries of qubit stabilizer codes. Adding one completion qubit per noncommuting pair preserves the gauged code space and its distance while keeping the checks Clifford.

Completion also preserves the low-density parity-check property with a constant-factor qubit overhead. We generalize completion to qudits and establish bounds on the Clifford-hierarchy level of the completed checks in prime dimensions.

Global commutation ensures that a fault-free round fixes the syndrome until the next fault and allows us to bound fault propagation independently of the number of measurement rounds. For qubit codes, we show that gauging and ungauging a distance-$d$ parent code implements a logical measurement with circuit fault distance $Ω(d)$ in $O(d)$ rounds.

We demonstrate the construction by gauging two toric codes into the $D(D_4)$ quantum double and back, with an explicit circuit whose circuit fault distance equals the parent code distance. Our results provide a framework for fault-tolerant logical measurements using commuting checks, with applications to magic-state preparation by lattice surgery.

items.title: High Rate Quantum Block Turbo Codes
items.summary:
Quantum Block Turbo Code is an iterative decoding technique for concatenated quantum error correction codes in product form.

In this paper, we study new high rate quantum block turbo codes with different constituent codes.

We examine the impact of the change of codes parameters and the order of constituent codes on turbo performance.
authors: Jean-Louis de Bougrenet de la Tocnaye

items.title: From Frobenius seeds to self-orthogonal modules over symmetric algebras
items.summary:
We construct finite-dimensional symmetric algebras admitting nonprojective self-orthogonal modules from Frobenius algebras equipped with a module satisfying explicit stable and homological conditions. The resulting modules have complexity three, and their stable endomorphism algebras are isomorphic to the algebra of dual numbers over the ground field.

The construction combines a variable input with a fixed auxiliary factor carrying the required twisting, and preserves the input through specified quotient and corner constructions. The proof combines derived induction, an obstruction to perfect factorization, and a cone construction over a Gorenstein triangular matrix algebra.

For a symmetric algebra and a self-orthogonal generator, we describe the derived category of the opposite endomorphism algebra through a recollement with a two-term $2$-symmetric dg algebra. For our counterexamples, it is formal and quasi-isomorphic to an explicit four-dimensional dg algebra.

Applications to cyclic coverings of a quantum exterior algebra yield connected examples with explicitly determined numbers of simple modules. The construction works over every field containing an element of infinite multiplicative order.

items.title: Lost in Rounding: bf16 Recurrent State Makes Hybrid Reasoning Models Think Longer
items.summary:
Hybrid reasoning models interleave attention with recurrent mixers such as Mamba-2 and Gated DeltaNet, whose state is cached between decoding steps. Prior work showed that storing this state in FP16 or INT8 with round-to-nearest (RTN) makes Mamba-2 and GDN hybrids more verbose, and that stochastic rounding (SR) fixes it. We study the other 16-bit format that serving engines expose, bf16, on six open hybrid reasoning models and 590 competition-math problems.

With bf16 RTN state, five of six models reason longer (geometric-mean length 1.07x to 1.27x; also under greedy decoding in the two models tested) and hit the 32K token cap more often. On Qwen3.5-9B, cap hits rise from 118 to 223 and accuracy falls from 85.6% to 70.8%. On LiveCodeBench, both models tested also reason longer and lose 12.6 and 13.4 points of pass@1.

Rerunning the capped items with a 128K budget halves the accuracy gap but does not close it (93.6% vs. 86.6%): bf16 runs that never finish are twice as common, and 85% of them are exact repetition loops. On Nemotron-Nano-9B-v2, by contrast, 30 of 31 extra caps finish at 128K, so the cost there is mostly extra tokens (exploratory).

Same-width bf16 SR removes the length increase in four of five affected models, restores Qwen3.5-9B to 87.6% and brings code length and pass@1 near FP32 levels, so the failure is mostly rounding bias, not missing resolution. With an integer-hash random generator, SR on Qwen3.5-9B matches FP32 on cap hits and accuracy (113 vs. 118; 85.6% for both) at the memory and decoding speed of bf16 RTN.

In the Nemotron-Nano-v2 lineage, SR on 25% of heads (an intermediate-decay band) removes the effect, while random heads and the top teacher-forced-KL octiles do not; in Nemotron-3 and Qwen3.5-9B the effect is spread across heads. We recommend that evaluations of hybrid models report the state dtype, cap rate and output length alongside accuracy.

items.title: Modular and Looping Quantum Photonic Processing Unit for Quantum Computing
items.summary:
Photonic processors are emerging as promising platforms in the race towards the realization of practical universal quantum computers. Several architectures with universal capabilities have been proposed for their implementation via a photonic platform, each with their own set of benefits and drawbacks.

In this work we propose an architecture for a universal photonic quantum computer. The proposed architecture is modular, allowing for a high degree of flexibility and scalability, and relies on a loop-based structure, significantly reducing the number of physical components required to implement it experimentally.

We prove that our architecture is universal, deterministic, and compatible with the quantum circuital model, as well as reprogrammable and capable of adaptive measurements. Furthermore, we showcase its functioning via numerical simulation on specific examples, by using machine learning techniques on a set of fundamental linear and nonlinear optical components to obtain some of the building blocks used in the architecture.

The obtained results can be used to highlight the benefits and the drawbacks of the proposed architecture, as well as the route for future developments towards its physical implementation.

items.title: A Universal Fault-Tolerant Quantum Computing Architecture with Globally Driven Atom Arrays
items.summary:
Scalable quantum computation requires reconciling programmability with simple, high-fidelity control. Here, we propose a universal fault-tolerant architecture using globally driven dual-species atom arrays.

In a hybrid neutral-atom system, interspecies Rydberg interactions enable qubit addressability without locally addressed quantum gates. We construct a universal native instruction set, Global Rydberg Atom Instruction Language (GRAIL), and show that crosstalk errors can be suppressed to the $10^{-4}$ level.

We compile surface-code error correction and magic state cultivation into GRAIL, and parallelize the compilation to suppress crosstalk. Under a hardware-inferred circuit-level noise model, we obtain an error-correction threshold of $1.43\%$ for the resulting quantum memory and a logical error rate below $10^{-9}$ for magic states cultivated at an experimentally accessible Rydberg Rabi frequency.

By replacing local gate addressing with atom-mediated selectivity, this architecture removes the associated calibration requirements, offering a route to simpler control for large-scale fault-tolerant neutral-atom computation.

items.title: Parameterized equivalence checking of quantum circuit generators via weighted automata
items.summary:
A generator builds a quantum circuit from the number of qubits and a bit string. We check a generator against a reference for all parameter values under six equivalence relations.

For ladder programs, we prove that above a computable threshold the circuit matrices form a uniform matrix product operator, a weighted automaton of dimension independent of the number of qubits. Equivalence reduces to the zeroness of a difference automaton, checked modulo primes.

The answer is a counterexample or "equal", exact or with a computed error bound. Experimentally, the method found errors missed by fixed-size checks and produced no incorrect verdicts.

items.title: MambaPD: Bidirectional Selective State Space Model for Parkinson's Disease Detection from Resting-State EEG
items.summary:
Typical diagnosis of Parkinson's disease (PD) occurs only after significant dopaminergic loss, while resting-state EEG abnormalities like alpha slowing and reduced coherence occur earlier. While many published EEG-based PD detectors claim accuracy greater than 95%, many use epoch-level splits which leak subject identity.

I introduce MambaPD, a bidirectional selective state space model for resting-state EEG-based PD detection, blending the channel mixing, patch tokenization and bidirectional Mamba encoder. It is compared with four baselines (TCN, BiLSTM with attention, EEGNet and a patch Transformer) in two public datasets (UNM, SanDiego) using subject-independent 5-fold cross-validation (checkpoints were selected on the held-out fold, so absolute estimates are optimistic).

On UNM the accuracy is between 0.67 and 0.71, and MambaPD (0.714) is not statistically distinguishable from the Transformer (0.715), and TCN (0.708), with the highest sensitivity (0.82), while the lowest specificity (0.52). For the smaller SanDiego cohort, accuracy is in the range of 0.60 to 0.70, with the highest scores (0.703) from TCN and the lowest (0.601) from EEGNet, while MambaPD scores 0.631, with the lowest specificity (0.46) among the five models.

The differences among the models on UNM are minor compared to the differences among folds. I report the whole pipeline, per-fold results, and the shortcomings of the protocol.

items.title: AutoQS: Automated Quantization Strategy Design with Large Language Models
items.summary:
Quantization reduces LLM deployment costs, but effective strategies must balance model quality and storage. LLM-driven search can automate strategy design through repeated proposal and evaluation.

This process must identify useful strategies within a limited evaluation budget. The key challenge is that \textit{actual quantization is expensive, while inexpensive proxies may not reflect quantized-model performance.} To address this challenge, we present AutoQS, an \textbf{Auto}mated \textbf{Q}uantization \textbf{S}trategy Design with LLMs.

AutoQS keeps weight precision fixed and searches group-size allocations across layers and operators under deployment constraints. Evaluation history guides coordinated LLM proposals, while deterministic validation ensures compatible allocations.

An inexpensive quality proxy evaluates candidates, and an candidate repository retains alternative allocations to inform subsequent proposals.
