items.title: Why Speculative Decoding Works Better Than Predicted on Sparse MoE Models
items.summary:
Speculative decoding (SD) accelerates autoregressive inference by leveraging the memory bound nature of decoding, verifying multiple draft tokens in a single forward pass. For mixture-of-experts (MoE) models, prior work predicts a concave speedup-batch size relationship, with gains peaking at intermediate batch sizes due to expert saturation.

We evaluate this across 10 sparse MoE models (30B--1T parameters, 8--512 experts) and find recent fine-grained models break this trend, showing higher speedup at low batch size. We find verification cost is governed not only by activated-expert bytes, but also by temporal overlap across draft tokens and GPU execution dynamics.

At low batch size, MoE layers in fine-grained models account for a much smaller share of runtime than of weights; on H100, kernel profiling attributes this mainly to higher bandwidth utilization of MoE kernels relative to attention, with L2 absorbing repeated reads of co-routed experts. Across draft tokens, routing overlap further reduces the unique experts activated during verification relative to independence assumptions.

We model this effect using a maximum-entropy Iterative Proportional Fitting (IPF) framework that predicts unique expert counts from routing-overlap statistics with less than 4\% error, and substantially narrows the gap to real-model curves and captures the qualitative low-batch trend from synthetic routing.

items.title: TableTune: Measured, Self-Correcting Draft-Length Tables for Dynamic Speculative Decoding
items.summary:
Speculative decoding speeds up large language model (LLM) serving only while the GPU has spare compute, so the best draft length, the number of tokens a small drafter guesses per step, shrinks as the batch grows. vLLM lets operators set the draft length for each batch size with a hand-written table, but nothing measures or corrects that table. We present TableTune.

Its tuner times the decoding step for every batch size and draft length on vLLM's own serving path and computes, in minutes, the table that maximizes throughput. Its controller, a vLLM plugin, tracks how many guesses are accepted in live traffic and rebuilds the table while serving.

We measure TableTune only against other ways to speculate. On an H100, the tuned table delivers at least 94% of the throughput of the best fixed draft length at every load in four of five drafter settings (88% in the fifth) without the operator having to know which length that is.

Against reimplementations of TurboSpec- and Nightjar-style control on the same engine, its worst-case loss is never higher than theirs, and with the EAGLE-3 drafter it is 3% against 9% and 12%. On a mixture-of-experts model, vLLM's documented table loses up to 18% and the tuned table at most 3%.

Starting from mistuned tables, the controller raises throughput by up to 58% (up to 45% on vLLM's default runner), and after a workload switch with the DFlash drafter it recovers 96% of a stale table's loss. In llm-d's optimized-baseline deployment as shipped, two Qwen3-32B replicas on four GPUs, the tuned table is up to 32% faster than a fixed draft length of 3 and up to 25% faster than vLLM's documented table at high load, and the controller raises the documented table's throughput by up to 29%.

items.title: PsiQuantum Unveils Optical Circuit Switch for AI Data Centers
items.summary:
Insider Brief

PsiQuantum has unveiled an 8×8 optical circuit switching demonstration built on its low-loss silicon photonics platform, originally developed for utility-scale quantum computing.

Company testing reported 1.2 dB insertion loss, 40 dB crosstalk performance and less than 3 milliseconds of reconfiguration time, without optical amplification.

PsiQuantum is sharing demonstration samples with selected prospective customers and plans to develop commercial products for AI data center connectivity while continuing its work on fault-tolerant quantum computers.

PRESS RELEASE — PsiQuantum today unveiled its Optical Circuit Switching (OCS) technology, demonstrating how the company’s advanced, low-loss silicon photonics platform can be applied to some of the most significant scaling challenges facing AI infrastructure.

AI systems are scaling faster than computing infrastructure, with increasingly large pools of compute placing enormous demands on the networks connecting them. As moving data efficiently between these systems becomes a fundamental constraint for continued AI scaling, the computing industry is increasingly turning to optics to provide faster, more efficient, and scalable connectivity.

PsiQuantum ‘s first publicly disclosed OCS is an 8×8-radix demonstration vehicle built on the low-loss, silicon photonics platform that the company has spent nearly a decade developing for utility-scale quantum computing. Testing conducted in PsiQuantum’s labs has shown typical results of 1.2 dB of insertion loss, 40 dB cross talk, and less than 3 ms of reconfiguration time, all exceeding initial targets set for these devices and without amplification.

items.title: NVision and HyperLight Partner to Develop Photonic Quantum Chips
items.summary:
Insider Brief

NVision has announced a peer-reviewed Nature paper on individually addressable organic molecular spin-photon interfaces and a partnership with HyperLight to integrate molecular qubits onto thin-film lithium niobate photonic integrated circuits.

The companies aim to combine NVision ’s molecular qubits with HyperLight’s photonic chip technology to develop quantum hardware with optical connections between qubits and compatibility with established foundry manufacturing processes.

NVision is targeting a demonstration of on-chip performance by the end of 2026, with its longer-term roadmap aiming for 1,000 physical qubits and then 1,000 logical qubits by 2030.

PRESS RELEASE — NVision , a quantum technology company, announced the publication of landmark peer-reviewed research in Nature and a strategic partnership with HyperLight Corporation (“HyperLight”), an industry leader in thin-film lithium niobate (TFLN) photonics. The companies will integrate NVision ’s thin-film molecular qubits directly onto advanced photonic integrated circuits (PICs). Together, these milestones establish a practical path to quantum computing at scale, using photonic connectivity to link quantum resources within and across processors. This opens a path toward millions of qubits on chips compatible with standard foundry manufacturing.

The Nature publication confirms the first ever individually addressable organic molecular spin-photon interface, which is the key ingredient for connecting stationary qubits with photons. Until now, molecular spins could not be individually and coherently controlled, preventing them from serving as true qubits. That barrier has now been broken: the core building block can be controlled at the single-molecule level. This opens a new path to scale, where molecular qubits can be deposited as thin films, much like OLED materials, directly on top of PICs, turning established photonic chip technology into a platform for scaling quantum computers.

“This proves what we’ve long believed: that organic chemistry offers a fundamentally better building block for quantum,” said Dr. Sella Brosh, CEO of NVision . “For years, the industry has been locked in a hardware race using modalities that would require decades and multi-billion-dollar proprietary fabrication facilities to achieve scale. With the creation of the world’s first manufacturable organic qubit, we now enter quantum’s molecular era, establishing a new architecture based on photonic connectivity from the get-go, with a clear path to scale through existing foundry infrastructure.”

items.title: Qarakal Quantum And Quantum Elements Receive BIRD Foundation Grant For Quantum Computing Innovation With a $2.4 Million Budget
items.summary:
Insider Brief

Quantum Elements and Qarakal Quantum were selected by the BIRD Foundation for a $2.4 million project to develop a quantum simulation platform for chemical reactions on material surfaces.

The collaboration will combine Qarakal’s superconducting quantum hardware with Quantum Elements’ digital-twin software and error-management tools to jointly optimize hardware and chemistry workflows.

The companies aim to build a validated prototype, benchmark chemistry models and quantum algorithms to investigate how quantum computing could complement existing catalyst simulation methods.

PRESS RELEASE — Quantum Elements and Qarakal Quantum today announced they have been selected by the Israel-U.S. Binational Industrial Research and Development (BIRD) Foundation to jointly develop a quantum simulation platform for understanding and designing the chemical reactions that occur on material surfaces.

The project, one of seven approved by the BIRD Foundation, has a budget of $2.4 million.

The project will combine Qarakal Quantum’s modular superconducting quantum hardware and hardware-software co-design approach with Quantum Elements’ software for advancing fault-tolerant quantum computing, using AI-driven co-design, error suppression, error correction and decoders.

items.title: Guest Post: Why Dedicated Compute Matters for AI and Quantum Computing
items.summary:
Guest Post By Christopher Miglino, CEO, Axe Compute

Every dollar going into AI infrastructure today is also a bet on what comes after it. Compute has become a strategic resource. Companies are spending billions to secure the processing power to build, train and run AI, and we’re still early: much of the global economy hasn’t put AI into its core operations yet.

But the infrastructure being built for AI is also the ground quantum will eventually stand on. That raises real questions about security, control and how to invest for a world where very different technologies run side by side.

My answer is dedicated compute. Enterprise AI customers already demand it, and it’s the flexibility businesses will need as quantum matures.

For most of the past decade, cloud economics favored sharing. Pooling resources across customers let providers reach scale, lift utilization and put sophisticated compute within reach of companies that couldn’t fund it upfront. That model works, and it will keep serving an enormous market.

But the math changes when compute becomes the thing your business runs on.

Picture a bank building proprietary trading models, or a pharmaceutical company running computational research. Their intellectual property lives in those workloads, alongside strict demands on performance, security and compliance. Their compute has become the business itself.

items.title: Dual DeltaNet: Value-Side Memory Reorganization for Linear Attention
items.summary:
Linear attention and state space models (SSMs) offer efficient alternatives to softmax attention by maintaining a fixed-size recurrent state, but this design requires careful management to preserve useful historical associations and limit interference. The delta rule helps reduce interference through correction of the value associated with each key, but it does not explicitly account for how related value features are distributed across the state.

We observe that a state $\boldsymbol{S}\in\mathbb{R}^{d_k\times d_v}$ can be viewed as a bank of $d_k$ addresses storing $d_v$-dimensional values. While a key-side read $\boldsymbol{S}^\top\boldsymbol{k}$ retrieves the value associated with $\boldsymbol{k}$, a value-side read $\boldsymbol{S}\boldsymbol{e}$ aggregates addresses whose stored value features match the selector $\boldsymbol{e}$.

Based on this observation, we propose Dual DeltaNet (DDN), which extends Kimi Delta Attention (KDA) with a two-sided delta rule. The key-side delta rule reads with the current key to correct its associated value, while the complementary value-side delta rule reads with selected features of the current value to reorganize the addresses it occupies.

We derive a chunkwise parallel training algorithm and a rank-2 recurrence that increases arithmetic intensity during inference. Compared with KDA, GDN-2, and Mamba-3, DDN achieves the strongest overall performance across language modeling, zero-shot downstream tasks, and retrieval, while incurring modest training and inference overhead relative to KDA.

Code: https://github.com/ReichtumQian/DualDeltaNet

items.title: Intel’s Classiq Deal May Signal a Pivot From Quiet Quantum Effort To Active Commercialization
items.summary:
Insider Brief

Intel ’s proposed acquisition of Classiq would move its decade-long quantum research effort toward commercialization by combining its hardware and manufacturing capabilities with Classiq ’s software and enterprise customers.

Intel plans to maintain Classiq ’s support for competing quantum hardware while exploring manufacturing and component partnerships with other quantum companies.

The companies expect the acquisition to close in the first half of 2027, subject to regulatory approvals, but provided no firm timetable for profitability or commercially useful quantum systems at scale.

Intel , a pioneer in quantum computing, has been relatively quiet about its technology and nearly silent about how it is pursing commercialization.

That silence has been shattered.

Intel executives said during a media briefing Tuesday that it is moving to turn more than a decade of quantum computing research into a business with its proposed acquisition of Classiq , adding software and enterprise customers to a hardware effort that has largely stayed out of the commercial spotlight.

items.title: LLM-PowerTrace: A Dataset of Time-Resolved GPU Power Traces for AI Compute
items.summary:
AI compute is becoming large and fast-changing electrical loads. Its impacts on data center infrastructure and power grids depend not only on total energy consumption, but also on how their power draw moves over sub-second to minute timescales, including peaks, ramps, and synchronized fluctuations across accelerators.

Existing energy benchmarks for large language models (LLMs) report aggregate quantities such as joules per token and rarely release the underlying time-series measurements, leaving these power dynamics poorly characterized and difficult to model. We introduce LLM-PowerTrace, an open dataset of time-resolved, per-GPU power traces for LLM fine-tuning and inference, sampled every 100\,ms on varying NVIDIA platforms paired with complete workload and system metadata.

For fine-tuning, LLM-PowerTrace profiles open model families spanning a wide range of model sizes and fine-tuning methods, together with controlled sweeps over batch size, sequence length, precision, parallelism, and checkpointing. For inference, it covers variations in concurrency, GPU frequency, KV-cache and weight quantization, prompt and output lengths, and request-arrival patterns.

LLM-PowerTrace profiles a set of open model families across a wide range of model sizes, and controlled sweeps over batch size, sequence length, precision, parallelism, and checkpointing for fine-tuning, and it sweeps concurrency, GPU frequency, KV cache and weight quantization, prompt and output lengths, and request arrival patterns for inference. Built upon power traces, we define power-grid-facing metrics as well as AI-compute power\&energy scaling law for extrapolating beyond the measured settings.

Together, LLM-PowerTrace provides a dataset foundation for modeling, forecasting, and managing the fast-changing electrical behavior of AI compute.

items.title: HotPOT: Operator Transformer with Heterogeneous Physics Experts for Large-Scale PDE Pre-training
items.summary:
Large-scale PDE pre-training trains a single model on the data from multiple partial differential equations (PDEs). However, adding heterogeneous PDEs with different governing equations, physical variables, and variable interactions does not always improve predictive performance across tasks.

Existing PDE mixture-of-experts models mitigate cross-task interference through learned routing, but typically use homogeneous expert architectures, making it difficult to directly reflect differences in state evolution across equations. We introduce HotPOT, an operator transformer with heterogeneous physics experts for large-scale PDE pre-training.

HotPOT uses a shared encoder to capture information common across PDEs, while each PDE family uses a neural-numerical expert that pairs a learnable predictor with a fixed numerical update containing no trainable parameters. Each predictor outputs the quantities required by its paired numerical update, which then computes the next state.

This design allows different PDEs to share a common encoder while retaining their own learnable predictors and numerical updates. Experiments across five PDE families and six settings show that HotPOT outperforms MoE-POT in all 24 matched-scale comparisons before and after fine-tuning, reducing rollout error by 50.7% on average.

Notably, the 17M model also surpasses substantially larger MoE-POT models, and the performance gains extend to zero-shot prediction under unseen physical conditions. Code is available at https://github.com/cruiseresearchgroup/HotPOT-code.

items.title: GAAC: Lossless KV Compression for Bandwidth-Efficient LLM Inference on Personal Devices
items.summary:
Weight-only, lossy quantization substantially reduces the storage and memory requirements for serving large language models (LLMs), but the growing key-value (KV) cache remains a bottleneck for long-context inference on personal devices. We present Group-Adaptive Additive Codec (GAAC), a lossless KV compression and serving system that exploits exponent redundancy to reduce storage and accelerate attention without introducing KV approximation. GAAC encodes BF16 exponents using calibrated per-channel base-plus-offset codes over contiguous ranges.

GAAC adapts code widths across small groups while preserving KV values bit-for-bit. A fused attention kernel reconstructs KV tiles on the fly, avoiding full-cache decompression. Block-wise compression and fixed-capacity slots support incremental cache updates and paged serving.

Across five tested models, GAAC achieves 1.405-1.407$\times$ lossless BF16 KV compression. We also study compression performance on low-precision tensors FP8 E4M3 caches ( 1.09-1.14$\times$) and E5M2 caches (1.25-1.30$\times$). On NVIDIA DGX Spark, GAAC accelerates decode attention at a 64K-token context by 1.19-1.27$\times$ and end-to-end W4A16 decode steps by 1.04-1.15$\times$.

In serving, it reduces resident KV memory by approximately 26% and increases aggregate throughput by 13-29% under comparable KV-memory budgets. On Apple M4, GAAC achieves 1.02-1.25$\times$ attention speedups, demonstrating portability beyond NVIDIA GPUs.

items.title: Nemotron 3.5 Super and Lightning: Open, Efficient Mixture-of-Experts Hybrid Mamba-Transformer Models for Agentic AI
items.summary:
We introduce Nemotron 3.5 Super and Nemotron 3.5 Lightning, open and efficient Mixture-of-Experts Hybrid Mamba-Transformer models designed for reasoning, long-context understanding, and agentic workloads. Super is a 120B-parameter, 12B-active multimodal model, while Lightning is a smaller 30B-parameter, 3B-active text model; both designed for efficient deployment. Both models combine large-scale distillation, long-context training, and native speculative decoding, while Super further incorporates Indic continued pretraining and agentic software-engineering mid-training.

We develop a comprehensive post-training pipeline spanning supervised fine-tuning and reinforcement learning (RLVR and RLHF), complemented in Super by specialized teacher training and multi- teacher on-policy distillation (MOPD). This transforms Super from a text-only base model into a multimodal agent capable of reasoning over text, images, video, and interactive tool environments. We further explore test-time scaling through parallel agent execution and self-verification.

Across training and deployment, we jointly optimize capability and efficiency. Indic continued pretraining improves Indian-language benchmarks by up to 9.82 percentage points, while agentic mid-training strengthens software-engineering capabilities and robustness across agent harnesses. The post-trained Super model achieves 51.78% on SWE-bench Pro, surpassing Nemotron 3 Ultra despite using approximately 4.6x fewer active parameters.

Post-training MTP boosting improves speculative- decoding acceptance length by up to 21.8% under probabilistic draft sampling, while NVFP4 quantization achieves 99.62% median accuracy recovery relative to BF16. Inference optimizations enable up to 4,856 output tokens/s/GPU on GB200 while sustaining at least 50 tokens/s/user.

items.title: GAUSS: A Workload-Aware Analytical and Monte-Carlo Simulator for LLM Inference Serving
items.summary:
Large language model (LLM) inference has become an operational workload that fleets must provision, monitor, and bill against latency service-level objectives (SLOs). A single throughput number cannot answer the questions operators actually face, because generative serving couples two phases with very different service characteristics, continuous batching reshapes the effective service process, and user-visible tail latency can degrade long before aggregate throughput saturates.

We present GAUSS, a workload-aware analytical and Monte-Carlo simulator that predicts the full distributions of time-to-first-token (TTFT) and time-between-tokens (TBT), together with the sustainable request rate, for a given workload, engine, and accelerator. GAUSS pairs calibrated, phase-specific latency surfaces for prefill and decode with a Lindley-recurrence model of queueing under stochastic arrivals and estimates performance by ensemble Monte-Carlo sampling rather than by replaying a single trace.

This lets GAUSS reason about workloads, routing policies, and hardware that have never been deployed, and to capture the latency tails that trace-driven simulators systematically under-sample. We describe the model and show how it supports operating-point selection, traffic segmentation, and shortest-remaining-processing-time scheduling capacity questions that trace-driven simulators cannot address.

items.title: Muon Makes the First Mixture-of-Experts Layer Harder to Balance
items.summary:
Many open mixture-of-experts (MoE) language models train with Muon instead of AdamW. Most balance the load with a bias on each expert's routing score, adjusted after every step. Their recipes disagree on whether Muon should also train the router.

In models with 55M and 108M active parameters, we measure how the optimizer changes the span of these biases, the largest minus the smallest in a layer. The span grows when all tokens favor the same experts, so it shows how hard a layer is to balance. At learning rates tuned on shorter runs, Muon raised the span of the first MoE layer at every seed, roughly doubling it on average, while the other layers changed much less.

The rise came from Muon on the rest of the network, whichever optimizer trained the router. In those runs, the inputs to the first router shared a direction, and soon after the warmup its busiest expert averaged four to seven times its fair share. Over the first 3,000 steps, subtracting the batch mean from these inputs removed this overload while barely changing the loss.

On the smaller model, halving Muon's learning rate removed most of the rise and slightly improved the loss. Moving only the router to AdamW made the loads shift more during the warmup and slightly raised the loss, so at this scale the results favor keeping the router on Muon.

items.title: Multi-State Linear Attention with Generalized Second-Order Routing
items.summary:
Self-attention plays a key role in long-sequence modeling, but its quadratic time complexity fundamentally limits the scaling of Large Language Models. Recently, Multi-State Linear Attention (MSLA) mechanisms have been proposed to make sequence modeling more efficient by splitting the context into segments and compressing each in its own memory state.

MSLA aggregates the information extracted from each memory state using only the mean alignment between a query and each segment's keys, ignoring how the alignment is distributed within the segment. In order to model the relevance of a segment to a query more comprehensively and incorporate the variance of the alignment in the aggregation, we propose MERLIN (MomEnt Routing for multi-state LINear attention), a method that tracks the first and second moments of each segment's keys.

Using the moments of keys, a query can recover both the mean and the variance of its alignment with each segment to perform a more content-aware aggregation of per-state readouts. Experiments on multi-state variants of Gated DeltaNet-1.3B and Mamba-2-780M show that MERLIN consistently outperforms existing aggregation methods on various long-context tasks.

In particular, MERLIN outperforms baselines on RULER needle-in-a-haystack and long-context QA (+8.3% for Gated DeltaNet-1.3B and +7.0% for Mamba-2-780M) and diverse subtasks in LongBench (+13.5% and +12.0%). It even outperforms baselines that consume 4x more memory.

MERLIN provides a simple and general routing mechanism for improving long-context capabilities of MSLA models.

items.title: QuantrolOx Raises €12 Million in Series A2
items.summary:
Insider Brief

QuantrolOx raised €12 million in a Series A2 round led by IW Capital, with EIC Fund co-investment, to expand its quantum hardware automation and training business internationally.

The company’s three products support quantum hardware development and calibration, practical workforce training, and superconducting quantum computing research and education.

The funding will support product deployments, expanded training offerings and growth of its U.S. team, following a Berkeley office opening and a five-year collaboration agreement with UC Berkeley.

PRESS RELEASE — QuantrolOx , University of Oxford spinout headquartered in Finland with offices in the UK, Netherlands, US and India, has raised €12 million in a Series A2 funding round led by IW Capital , with co-investment from the European Innovation Council (EIC) Fund . The round also includes participation from Voima Ventures , Serendipity Capital , Hoxton Ventures , and Transpose Capital .

The investment will accelerate QuantrolOx ’s commercial growth and international expansion, including its growing presence in North America following the opening of its first US office in Berkeley, California. The round brings QuantrolOx’s total funding to ~$31million or ~€28million.

As quantum computing moves towards industrial-scale development, two major challenges remain: automating increasingly complex quantum hardware and training the workforce needed to build and operate it.

items.title: GTFormer: A Syntax-Free Graph Network Alternative to Transformers for 8192$\times$ Length Extrapolation in Linear Time
items.summary:
Self-attention mechanisms have established the Transformer as the dominant backbone across natural language processing, source code intelligence, and automated theorem proving.

However, all-to-all pairwise token comparison enforces a quadratic $\mathcal{O}(N^2)$ compute and memory barrier alongside severe softmax attention dilution as sequence length $N$ scales beyond the training horizon.

Inspired by recent advances in algebraic graph learning (\textbf{WPNet}), this work introduces \textbf{GTFormer}, a syntax-free hierarchical Graph Neural Network (GNN) that replaces flat self-attention for general long-context sequence modeling.

GTFormer organizes raw token streams into a bounded-degree hierarchy combining a balanced binary reduction tree ($\lceil \log_2 N \rceil$ depth), horizontal boundary-bridging shift edges, random expander shortcuts, multi-channel convex highway gating, and a top-down broadcast pass.

Across eight long-context code, log, and multi-hop retrieval benchmarks trained exclusively on sequences of length $N \le 512$, GTFormer extrapolates zero-shot to $N = 4{,}194{,}304$ ($8192\times$) on a single commodity GPU in linear $\mathcal{O}(N)$ memory, maintaining near-perfect accuracy where standard and RoPE Transformers suffer from out-of-distribution attention collapse and out-of-memory exhaustion.

items.title: CRISP: Co-designing Pruning and Scheduling for Efficient MoE Inference on Edge Servers
items.summary:
Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) inference on memory-constrained edge platforms is often dominated by expert-weight movement rather than computation. Although each token activates only a small subset of experts, routing is input-dependent, so all experts must remain accessible and memory movement dominates latency.

Existing approaches such as uniform pruning and expert dropping overlook two properties of MoE execution: expert combinations are highly skewed in frequency, and experts contribute asymmetrically within each combination. We present CRISP, a combination-aware framework that co-designs pruning and runtime scheduling for efficient MoE serving on memory-constrained edge platforms.

CRISP reorders neurons by importance so one stored expert can support multiple execution widths, assigns differentiated execution to hot, warm, and cold combinations based on frequency and expert role, and exploits heterogeneous widths to overlap expert loading with computation. Across Mixtral-8x7B and DeepSeek-MoE-16B, CRISP improves throughput by up to $2.1\times$ at the same memory budget while limiting accuracy loss to 3.6\% relative to full-width inference.

Our results highlight that efficient edge MoE serving requires jointly optimizing which expert capacity is preserved and how expert execution is scheduled.

items.title: Channel Selection for Mixture-of-Experts Decoding Needs No Calibration Data
items.summary:
Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) models are bottlenecked by loading routed-expert weights from memory during interactive decoding at small batch sizes. Because most intermediate channels in a routed expert contribute little to any single token, channel selectors predict which channels matter and read only their weights, typically keeping channels above a threshold calibrated on offline data.

We show that channel selection needs no calibration data. First, a calibrated threshold does not fix how much a selector reads, because the number of channels passing it varies across inputs; Prox with thresholds calibrated for an 18% read budget actually reads only 12.9% on average across our benchmarks.

Second, top-k keeps each token's k highest-scoring channels and needs no calibration data. At the calibrated budget, a selector's top-k version matches or beats its threshold version on the same score in 40 of 43 comparisons at 13% and 18% budgets, including all 23 on generation tasks.

The top-k versions also avoid the repetition-loop collapse that calibrated thresholds cause on Gemma 4. Calibrating a threshold thus provides neither of the two things selectors use it for: a known read budget and a consistent accuracy gain at that budget.

We furthermore introduce a reader built entirely from the model's weights, which screens channels with a ternary sketch and recovers the skipped ones with a low-rank map. Across three post-trained MoE models, our reader retains 98.1% of full-model accuracy at 17.8% of routed-expert reads, with Triton kernels running MoE blocks 1.60 to 1.90x faster than optimized vLLM at batch one and up to 2.69x at larger batches on the same three models.

items.title: CoS-VQ: Coordinated Shared-Scale Vector Quantization for Large Language Models
items.summary:
Large language models (LLMs) require substantial memory, motivating low-bit weight quantization for efficient deployment. Existing vector quantization (VQ) methods often improve accuracy by increasing the effective coding dimension, which can complicate independent lookup and local codeword updates.

We propose CoS-VQ (Coordinated Shared-Scale Vector Quantization), which preserves low-dimensional codewords while jointly optimizing hard indices and their shared scale across positions. The key challenge is scale-induced coupling: the optimal scale depends on the entire codeword combination and, in turn, changes candidate rankings across positions, so pointwise updates can stall even after scale re-optimization.

CoS-VQ collects candidates at multiple probe scales and constructs a tangent separable upper bound for the residual-aware quadratic objective. By reducing candidate comparisons to lower envelopes of lines over positive scales, it identifies finitely many representative intervals for joint index--scale updates without exhaustively enumerating codeword combinations.

On Qwen3.8-27B, CoS-VQ outperforms QTIP and LLVQ on the evaluated language modeling, coding, and reasoning benchmarks. Ablations from the same initialization further show larger gains from joint updates than from scale-only refinement, highlighting joint selection as an alternative to increasing codeword dimensionality.

The code is available at https://github.com/xzktx003/Cos_VQ.

items.title: Beyond Binary Quantum Computing: Exploring Higher-Dimensional Qudits
items.summary:
Quantum computing is often talked about in terms of qubits, the quantum equivalent of a classical binary bit. But what if the most efficient way to process quantum information is not always binary?

At the University of Rochester, Associate Professor of Physics Machiel Blok and his research group are exploring that question through work on superconducting qudits, quantum systems that can encode information across multiple energy levels instead of just two. Their research examines whether these higher-dimensional systems could provide advantages for quantum simulation, quantum error correction, and future quantum computing architectures by using more of the quantum states that already exist within the hardware itself.

Matching quantum hardware to the problems of nature

According to Machiel, one of the motivations behind qudit research comes from an observation about nature.

Many physical systems are not naturally binary. Atoms, molecules, vibrational modes, and quantum fields often contain multiple accessible states. If the systems that researchers want to simulate are inherently multi-level, it may be advantageous to use a quantum processor that reflects that structure.

The Rochester team studies superconducting circuits similar to those used throughout the quantum computing industry. Instead of using only two energy states as a qubit, they investigate how additional states can be accessed, controlled, and used for computation.

Their goal is not necessarily to replace qubits, but to understand when higher-dimensional quantum systems may provide a more efficient way to represent information and solve a problem.

items.title: EnergyCal: Taming Loss Spikes in Muon-Family Optimizers for Sparse MoE Training
items.summary:
Sparse mixture-of-experts (MoE) language-model training can exhibit large loss spikes with Muon-family optimizers. We introduce EnergyCal, a lightweight rule that attenuates routed-expert updates according to the normalized squared Frobenius norm of their finite-step Newton-Schulz directions.

EnergyCal leaves the spectral transform unchanged and adds no persistent optimizer state. We evaluate it on a 4B-parameter MoE model.

Against a development-selected, lower-learning-rate MuonH recipe, EnergyCal-MuonH reduces mean thresholded loss-spike burden by 99.51% and final geometric-mean perplexity by 4.06%, with a modest throughput cost. With plain Muon at matched nominal learning rate and weight decay, the reduction in mean spike burden averages 95.98% across the two tested exponents, accompanied by small endpoint improvements.

These findings support stabilization both with and without Hyperball in the evaluated setting.

items.title: From QCCD Trapped-Ion Hardware to Quantum Compilers: Capabilities, Architectures, and Compilation
items.summary:
Shuttling-based trapped-ion quantum computers (QCCD) rank among the most mature hardware platforms. Existing and envisaged devices exhibit architectural differences in terms of register layout and connectivity.

Platform-specific compilers are required to translate quantum circuits into resource-optimized hardware-level command chains. Hardware platforms and compiler software stacks are mostly developed independently of one another by different research communities.

This work aims to bridge these communities by abstracting QCCD architectures and native operations, enabling computer scientists to address compilation problems using generic methods without requiring a deep background in the physical operating principles of the platform. The resulting design space is organized into a small set of architectural archetypes, each posing its own compilation problem.

We then select and apply compilation methods to one- and two-dimensional QCCD architectures, finding that the routing overhead scales approximately cubically with the number of qubits for the one-dimensional architecture and approximately quadratically for the two-dimensional one. Extending this to compilation with a quantum error-correction layer reveals additional differences and similarities between the physical and logical levels.

We conclude that co-design is a requirement rather than an option, and this work provides the vocabulary, archetypes, and compilation abstraction it needs.

items.title: DCKV: Learned Transform Coding of the Prompt KV Cache in Hybrid Language Models
items.summary:
Hybrid language models keep a key-value (KV) cache only in their few full-attention layers, but this cache is still the part of a prompt's state that grows with the prompt and that must be stored or moved to reuse it.

We present DCKV, a differentiable codec for the KV cache and the first KV-cache codec that is trained end to end.

Its transform, its quantizer and its entropy models, which are conditioned on the prompt tokens and on already decoded neighbouring positions, are optimized together against the frozen language model, both for the code length that the entropy models assign and for the change of the model's output.

On Qwen3.5-2B, DCKV stores a compressed token in more than 55 times fewer bytes than bf16 at a loss of at most 1.8 points on three long-context benchmarks, and in more than 100 times fewer bytes at a loss of at most 3.6 points.

items.title: TDLM: Adaptive Temporal Integration for Diffusion Language Models
items.summary:
Masked diffusion language models repeatedly compute representations for unresolved tokens, but conventional denoisers do not explicitly retain these representations for reuse across steps. We introduce Temporal Self-Conditioning Diffusion Language Model (TDLM), which lets each unresolved position attend to its own history of hidden representations within a frozen denoiser.

This gives later predictions access to computation already performed. Training uses self-generated trajectories and a simple cross-entropy objective for tokens revealed between consecutively sampled decoding steps, while causal temporal attention permits parallel evaluation during training.

On LLaDA, the temporal modules add only approximately 0.84% trainable parameters. Across LLaDA and Dream, the main comparison shows up to 7.15$\times$ faster generation than the corresponding original diffusion language model, with competitive answer quality on the evaluated tasks.

These results motivate temporal memory as a practical way to make more effective use of repeated denoising computation.

items.title: Qubit-environment entanglement in pure dephasing dynamics for mixed initial states
items.summary:
Decoherence of qubits is one main limitation in quantum information processing, where the qubits themselves can be mixed because of decoherence and additional decoherence may generated through interactions with a bath. Here, we present a complete study of qubit-environment entanglement in the case of interactions that lead to pure dephasing of the qubit by allowing the initial state of the qubit to be mixed, exceeding previous restrictions.

We find that the criteria for separability that hold for pure initial states of the qubit are reduced to witness status. Yet, the evolution of the witnesses reflects the array of features that entanglement can exhibit in the mixed case but are forbidden in the pure-qubit case.

Most notably, this includes sudden birth of entanglement as the initial phase of the evolution is typically separable. Moreover, there is a stark numerical advantage to the study of entanglement for large environments when using the witness rather than the traditional measures available.

We include the study of entanglement generated between a spin qubit and a sparse spin environment to illustrate the peculiarities of the evolution of entanglement in this case, as well as to emphasize the level of reliability of the entanglement witness.

items.title: LRMoE: Demand-Side Load Re-Calibration for Efficient MoE Training on Memory-Constrained Nodes
items.summary:
Sparse Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) models offer scalable capacity for Web applications, but uneven routing creates computation and communication bottlenecks. Existing placement and replication methods redistribute this workload, yet additional expert copies compete with token-related buffers for limited GPU memory.

We present LRMoE, a memory-aware MoE training system that jointly recalibrates backward demand and balances the retained workload. During forward execution, it plans retention quotas and expert placement under resource constraints while preserving all routed computations.

During backpropagation, a load recalibration metric estimates each token-expert pair's contribution to the expert update and selects pairs within these quotas. A capacity-aware routing algorithm distributes retained pairs among eligible instances of their original experts.

Physical compaction then forms smaller communication payloads and variable-size grouped GEMMs, reducing backward traffic, computation, and execution-buffer demand. Experiments on Qwen3-30B-A3B and GLM4.5-106B-A12B show that LRMoE reduces cumulative MoE-layer training time to fixed-loss targets by 21.2-44.8% relative to SYMI.

items.title: HiLo-RD: Cross-Budget Self-Distillation for Masked Diffusion Language Models
items.summary:
We propose HiLo-RD (High-to-Low Budget Representation Distillation) to improve masked diffusion language models (MDLMs) under a limited generation budget. Unlike autoregressive models, MDLMs choose both what to generate and where to commit it. This creates two coupled challenges: predicting useful content before reasoning is complete, and deciding when to fix answer tokens that shape later predictions.

We identify budget-induced premature commitment: even when a correct solution fits, the model can fix answer fragments near the window boundary before resolving intermediate steps. These fragments become context for later predictions and redirect subsequent reasoning. Existing post-training methods do not directly transfer the stronger trajectories that the same model follows with a larger window.

HiLo-RD addresses this gap by (1) pairing large-window teacher states with cropped small-window views and (2) matching their hidden representations at committed positions. This supervision guides both token prediction and commitment order without an external teacher. Across mathematics benchmarks, HiLo-RD improves low-budget accuracy and shortens responses; these gains extend to code generation without code-domain training.

On GSM8K, accuracy rises by 9.4 percentage points as mean readable length falls by about 25%. Attention diagnostics and fixed-budget order interventions support the proposed mechanism. Together, these results show that large-window reasoning can improve small-window decoding.

items.title: OpenAI Computing Claim Faces Review, Raising Questions About Quantum Advantage
items.summary:
Insider Brief

OpenAI has enlisted outside researchers to examine an AI-generated proof that it says overturns a longstanding assumption about the difficulty of certain computing problems.

The claim could affect some assumptions used to assess quantum computing’s advantages, but does not itself establish a practical improvement in classical computing.

A separate academic collaboration will examine OpenAI ’s claimed mathematical existence proofs for quantum field theories, including quantum chromodynamics.

OpenAI has enlisted outside researchers to examine an AI-generated proof that it says overturns a longstanding assumption about computing’s limits, according to a company news release that identifies three scientific advances under scrutiny.

The claim concerns the Exponential Time Hypothesis , or ETH, which describes how quickly the difficulty of certain logic problems grows. The claim could matter to quantum computing because predictions of a quantum computer’s advantage sometimes depend on assumptions about what ordinary computers can — and cannot — do.

A group led by Russell Impagliazzo and Ramamohan Paturi of the University of California, San Diego , and Ryan Williams of MIT will verify and explain the work, according to OpenAI’s announcement . Impagliazzo and Paturi helped formulate the hypothesis. OpenAI says the proof has been checked in Lean, a mathematical verification system, and released for public examination.

items.title: IBM Connects Two 120-Qubit Processors With 99% State-Transfer Fidelity
items.summary:
Insider Brief

IBM researchers linked two 120-qubit quantum processors with four superconducting cables, demonstrating connections that could support larger modular quantum computers.

The links achieved average quantum state-transfer fidelity of 99% and enabled operations and entanglement between qubits on separate processors.

Complete operations between processors averaged 94.75% fidelity, with further improvements needed in qubit stability, magnetic shielding and manufacturing before scaling the approach.

IBM researchers connected two quantum processors through four superconducting cables, demonstrating a way to build larger quantum computers from separate chips.

The links transferred quantum states with an average fidelity of 99% and supported operations between computing elements on different processors, according to a study posted on the preprint server arXiv . The team also created entangled states spanning the chips, including two pairs generated at the same time through neighboring connections.

The results address a practical problem in quantum computing: how to make separate processors work together without losing the fragile information that gives the machines their potential. Connecting modules could let developers expand a computer beyond the limits of a single chip.

items.title: Balanced State Subspaces for Mamba-2 State Compression
items.summary:
Mamba-2 compresses all context into a fixed-size recurrent state that dominates decoding memory and bandwidth. Existing compressors quantize state values or prune state coordinates, scoring each channel independently in the native basis.

We examine trained Mamba-2 states and find that energy is almost rank-one, but the output does not read the energetic directions: energy concentrates in a bias-like direction accumulated by the recurrence, while the content the output reads lives in a low-dimensional subspace that is not aligned with the state's coordinates. Even output-aware scores are computed coordinate by coordinate, so they miss the directions that determine the input--output map.

Compression should therefore target the write--read subspace rather than individual coordinates. We propose \method{}, a post-training transform that instantiates balanced truncation with full controllability and observability Gramians and applies the rotation exactly via Mamba-2's scalar-identity transition.

Because the useful rank varies widely across layers, we further introduce HARP, which allocates ranks per layer from the Hankel spectrum and protects retrieval-sensitive layers, improving both perplexity and retrieval over uniform budgets. Calibration takes a single forward pass, an order of magnitude faster than GHOST's released protocol, with lower peak memory.

With HARP, \method{} halves the state dimension at an average WikiText-2 perplexity increase of $0.3$ points ($1.8\%$) across 130M--2.7B, versus $1.6$ ($9.3\%$) for GHOST, and the gap widens at 25\% retention.

items.title: Effective Noise Thresholds for Reliable Quantum Approximation Optimisation Algorithm under Noisy Environment
items.summary:
Variational quantum algorithms are leading candidates for practical utilisation on noisy intermediate-scale quantum (NISQ) processors, but accumulating noise bounds the usefulness of circuit depths. For the quantum approximate optimisation algorithm (QAOA), this trade-off has mostly been addressed by searching for the best depth for a given device.

In this work, we consider the inverse question: how much noise each depth can tolerate. Using GPU-accelerated noisy QAOA simulations for MaxCut on three graph families with 6 to 18 vertices, depths up to 10 and three noise channels, we fit the approximation ratios with a generalised logistic surface.

We propose the effective noise threshold as the inflection boundary of the logistic surfaces, a noise boundary separating reliable and unreliable QAOA approximation regimes. In general, the threshold decreases as depth rises, indicating that deeper circuits demand for stricter noise requirement for reliable approximation.

Its best and worst values over depth divide the noise axis into three regions: every depth remains effective, depth must be chosen with care, or no depth induces effective optimisation. Assessing on the ibm_marrakesh processor, although modelled gate errors understate factual noise, the threshold modeling remains beneficial in informing qualitative depth-dependence structure and identifying dominating noise channel in noisy QAOA.

items.title: Folding Attention Biases into Keys Makes Compacted KV Caches Run on Standard Kernels
items.summary:
Attention Matching (AM) compacts a KV cache by keeping some keys per head, refitting their values and adding a bias to each kept key's logit. FlashAttention and vLLM's paged caches have no input for it.

We fold the bias into the keys along one closed-form direction per head, fitted on context queries, giving a plain cache with AM's size and head dimension and the model's own query path; the output error is bounded by how far each query's projection on that direction is from 1. With equal per-head budgets, unmodified vLLM serves folded caches through a KV connector, matching Hugging Face's answers on all 51 Qwen3-4B questions and its greedy output on 180 of 200 Qwen3-14B LongBench samples.

With equal budgets on QuALITY (Qwen3-1.7B, 4B, 8B, Llama-3.1-8B) and LongHealth (three Qwen3 models), the fold is within noise of AM's accuracy in 13 of 14 settings, with lower KL to the full cache than dropping the bias in all 12 where both ran. Under the published per-head budgets, on Qwen3-4B, its Instruct-2507 variant and Llama-3.1-8B, it is within noise of AM in 9 of 10, no longer beats dropping the bias in KL, and the two each win once in accuracy.

items.title: WAKMan: Workload Aware KVCache Manager
items.summary:
Prefix caching enables a Large Language Model (LLM) servers to reuse the Key-Value (KV) states and accelerate prefill computation stage for requests that share a prefix with earlier prompts, thus reducing latency and serving cost. With limited memory resource, the KV cache eviction policy becomes a decisive factor in determining the overall benefits of prefix caching.

Production traffic may have single-turn, multi-turn, agentic, or a mixture of any combination of these request types. Our findings indicate that agentic steps return within seconds and favor recency, while popular prompts and long conversations return after many other requests and favor frequency.

Across 20 mixes, no single policy is always best: vLLM's default strategy LRU provides 12% higher cache hits as compared to the frequency-oriented S3FIFO on agentic-heavy mixes but trails it by up to 22% elsewhere, and even a single workload parameter can flip the winner even for any particular mix. We present WAKMan, a workload-aware KV cache manager that picks its eviction policy from live traffic without knowing request types or reading prompts.

It improves hit rate over LRU by 5 percentage points on average, with the lowest mean and worst-case optimality gap of all policies.

items.title: Intel to Acquire Classiq to Create a Full-stack Quantum Computing Platform
items.summary:
Insider Brief

Intel has agreed to acquire quantum software company Classiq, combining its algorithm synthesis platform with Intel’s silicon spin-qubit hardware and software to build a full-stack quantum computing business.

Classiq’s platform automates quantum circuit design, enabling developers to create applications without deep expertise in the underlying hardware.

The acquisition is expected to close in the first half of 2027, subject to regulatory approvals and customary conditions, with Intel planning to maintain Classiq’s support for multiple hardware platforms.

PRESS RELEASE — Intel Corporation today announced that it has entered into a definitive agreement to acquire Classiq, a leading provider of quantum computing software. The combination of Classiq’s synthesis platform with Intel’s spin-qubit manufacturing and existing software would create a user-friendly full-stack quantum computing platform, enabling the promising technology to mature into a mainstream computing business.

More than forty years ago, the invention of Electronic Design Automation (EDA) and Computer‑Aided Design (CAD) software transformed silicon chip design and classical computing by providing a common software platform that could abstract the ability to design chips from the complexity of the underlying hardware. Classiq plays a similar role in quantum computing, providing a unifying software platform that is agnostic to the underlying qubit modality and hardware. Providing this high-level abstraction enables quantum computing to scale beyond custom hand-crafted circuits and applications to become a mainstream computing platform.

Classiq’s synthesis platform brings complementary assets to Intel’s already strong quantum hardware and software capabilities developed over the last decade. Since 2015, Intel has been investing in the development of quantum computing, and today it is the only company capable of producing qubit chips and complex cryogenic control electronics at-scale, using equipment and processes common to conventional silicon-based semiconductor manufacturing.

items.title: Towards Quantum Computation of Bulk FeO
items.summary:
Quantum computation offers a promising path towards efficient calculations of the electronic structure of correlated materials. The properties of iron-based materials, which are key for advancing geological and astrophysical understanding, are notoriously difficult to calculate with classical computers.

However, despite the many recent advances in quantum computing on near intermediate scale quantum hardware, a full treatment of the electronic structure of high-$Z$ atoms or molecules remains challenging. Here, we investigate the ground-state properties of molecular FeO and Fe$_2$O$_2$ model Hamiltonians using classical exact diagonalization, Variational Quantum Eigensolver (VQE), and Sample-based Quantum Diagonalization (SQD).

The experimental quintet ground state of FeO is recovered classically and with quantum algorithms, while a nonet ground state is recovered for Fe$_2$O$_2$. Although raw VQE does not achieve chemical accuracy for the ground state of FeO or Fe$_2$O$_2$, SQD with two connectivity shells recovers the exact ground energy for both molecules utilizing remarkably few quantum computational resources.

Overall, our results indicate that $ab \; initio$-informed low-energy models of correlated materials, combined with SQD, offer a new alternative for scaling up calculations of ground-state properties of strongly correlated solids on existing quantum hardware.

items.title: Quantitative Generalization Bounds for Multi-Layer Transformers: A Few Long Strings can Beat Many Short Ones
items.summary:
Transformer-based language models exhibit an astonishing capacity to generalize to longer and more difficult problem instances than those seen in training. However, theoretical understanding of this phenomenon still lags behind.

Unlike most machine learning models, the generalisation abilities of transformers inherently require considering two axes. On one hand, one must examine in-distribution statistical generalisation, which concerns the ability of a model to broaden a function from training samples to novel samples of the same distribution.

On the other hand, given the sequential nature of language data, one must also consider length generalisation, which reflects whether a model trained on inputs of a given length can extrapolate to longer ones.These two notions have mostly been studied separately, leaving open how they interact. In this work, we give a joint treatment of both axes for fixed-precision transformers.

We give generalisation guarantees in terms of the parameter sizes of the involved models, as well as the quantization space and the alphabet size that supply the sequences. Finally, we illustrate how the requirements in the sample count and training length trade off.

In particular, we find that increasing training length can be exponentially more efficient than increasing the sample size. Experiments support predictions of the theory.

items.title: DuplexTune: Coupled-State Replay for Memory-Efficient Mixture-of-Experts Adaptation
items.summary:
Sparse expert execution does not remove the stored states needed to adapt a mixture-of-experts language model. We present DuplexTune, a framework for replaying coupled hidden states through pretrained attention and expert modules.

Trainable width bridges connect two residual streams to the backbone. Bridge warm-up precedes backbone adaptation, with router weights kept frozen.

We analyze the implicit state-recovery equation and identify the convergence and replay conditions needed for reconstruction. On Qwen1.5-MoE-A2.7B, the single-H800 evaluation reports 38.8 GB peak memory, versus 64.8 GB for supervised fine-tuning with checkpointing, and throughput of 25.1 versus 19.9 samples/s.

DuplexTune achieves 67.2% MMLU, 75.6% GSM8K, and 7.69 MT-Bench, with a weaker multilingual score than the checkpointed baseline. The results characterize a configuration-dependent tradeoff among state storage, throughput, and adaptation quality.

items.title: $κ$-Parametrized Boltzmann Distribution Sampling on Quantum Approximate Optimization Algorithm
items.summary:
Generative models use training data to produce new samples that resemble the original, with applications in classification and recommendation systems. Restricted Boltzmann Machines (RBMs) are at the core of generative models but suffer from the computational intractability of training, which relies on sampling an unknown Boltzmann Distribution (BD).

The Quantum Approximate Optimization Algorithm (QAOA) can assist RBM training, potentially providing benefits over strictly classical strategies. One particular problem is determining the quantum circuit depth for an arbitrary problem size that yields the expected sampling results.

In this study, we evaluate QAOA-assisted sampling of BDs using Qiskit's Aer Simulator by analysing the inverse effective temperature of the distribution, $κ$, for tractable problem sizes. The results provide numerical evidence, based on Qiskit Aer simulations, that parameterized annealing-scheduled QAOA (PAQ-QAOA) can approximate RBM Boltzmann sampling for the tractable instances considered, while hardware performance and scaling remain open questions.
authors: João Marcos Cavalcanti de Albuquerque Neto

items.title: From Denoising Dynamics to Endpoint Uncertainty in Diffusion Language Models
items.summary:
Predictive uncertainty in stochastic language-model inference can be characterized by repeatedly sampling an input and measuring the distribution of outputs. This requires multiple complete generations. Masked diffusion language models expose another source of information: the evolution of the output during denoising.

We ask whether convergence within diffusion trajectories is associated with uncertainty across their final outputs, or endpoints. We study four masked diffusion language models on four reasoning benchmarks, collecting 20 generations per question and 32,000 denoising trajectories in total. Within each trajectory, we measure within-run concentration as the area under the curve describing stable resolution of the eventual output.

Across repeated trajectories, we measure endpoint-distribution uncertainty. Stronger within-run concentration is associated with lower endpoint entropy after accounting for model and dataset ($β=-0.222$, $p<10^{-25}$). This association persists for multi-token outputs and when reweighting positive-entropy cases.

The relationship is asymmetric: high within-run concentration almost exclusively accompanies concentrated endpoint distributions, whereas lower concentration occurs under both concentrated and competing endpoint regimes. This relationship strengthens as denoising proceeds. Features from a single denoising run predict whether independent held-out runs will concentrate on a common endpoint or produce competing endpoints.

These results connect dynamics within individual denoising runs to variability across repeated inference. Within-trajectory dynamics contain information about whether independent repetitions will concentrate on a common endpoint or produce competing endpoints, providing a route towards estimating endpoint-distribution properties with fewer complete generations.

items.title: Quantum Art Research Outlines More Efficient Quantum Approach to Wave Modeling
items.summary:
Insider Brief

Quantum Art presented research on a quantum algorithm that uses known wave physics to simplify large-scale wave simulations, with potential applications in telecommunications, seismic modeling and engineering.

The method constructs physically allowed wave states directly, aiming to avoid computational overhead that limits existing quantum approaches as the modeled region grows.

The company estimates that some simulations requiring 10¹⁸–10²¹ classical grid points could potentially use roughly 100 qubits, although practical implementation depends on further hardware advances.

PRESS RELEASE — – Quantum Art , a developer of full-stack, fault tolerant quantum computers based on trapped-ion qubits and a proprietary, dynamically reconfigurable multi-core architecture, recently presented new research, detailed in this paper , that solves wave-propagation problems long thought intractable for classical supercomputers – unlocking new simulation capabilities for seismic modeling, structural engineering, and materials science.

Simulating how waves, from radio signals to sound, travel through space demands enormous computing power, and that demand grows sharply when the area being modeled gets larger but the level of detail cannot be reduced. The stakes are real for industries that depend on precision: telecom carriers predict network coverage, engineers model how buildings and materials hold up under stress, and geophysicists track how seismic waves move through the earth. The research explains the science behind the large-scale wave-simulation results the company previously demonstrated in May through a joint project with a leading Israeli governmental research and development agency.

Quantum computers hold a key advantage here: they can represent extremely large problems using relatively few qubits. Most existing quantum methods, however, treat a wave problem as a vast, generic mathematical puzzle. They solve a huge system of equations by brute force, with little regard for what the equations describe. Waves follow strict physical rules: a wave of a given frequency travels at a fixed speed in a given medium, so every direction it could possibly travel in can be pictured as the hand of a clock. Because the speed is fixed, every hand is the same length, so their tips can only trace out one perfect circle. Anything off that circle is physically impossible. Prior methods still expend effort searching far outside that circle, checking possibilities that the physics has already ruled out. As a result, they tend to slow dramatically or lose their quantum advantage, especially on a large-scale problem.

items.title: Report: UK’s £30 Million Quantum Testbed Program Helps Suppliers Advance Toward Commercial Deployment
items.summary:
Insider Brief

Britain’s £30 million quantum computing testbed program helped seven suppliers deploy prototype systems across five computing approaches, gaining experience in installation, operation and customer support.

The initiative supported hardware development, new supplier partnerships and expanded UK operations, with collaborative projects securing £4.6 million in follow-on funding.

Six testbeds entered independent technical evaluation, with the main testing program due to conclude in the second quarter of 2027 to assess performance and explore potential applications.

Britain’s £30 million quantum computing testbed program helped seven hardware suppliers develop systems for use outside their own laboratories, offering lessons in installation, reliability and customer support as the country begins a broader evaluation of the machines, according to a new report.

The National Quantum Computing Centre’s Phase 1 report , released recently, identifies its role as an early customer as a central benefit of the initiative. Suppliers received funding and technical support, but also faced the practical demands of delivering working equipment, documenting its operation and preparing it for outside scrutiny.

The program established seven prototype systems across five approaches to quantum computing at the Harwell Campus in Oxfordshire. Its next phase, conducted with the University of Edinburgh ’s Quantum Software Lab, is evaluating performance and exploring which systems may suit particular computational problems.

items.title: Measurement-dependent reduction of open dynamics in the quantum phase estimation algorithm: the visible subspace and the damped Fejér kernel
items.summary:
For the quantum phase estimation (QPE) algorithm we study the minimal space of observables that is sufficient to predict the entire output distribution under open dynamics of the counting register. Building on the general Krylov theory of reduction, we compute the structure of this space explicitly for the full Fourier measurement.

The outcome probabilities are determined by cyclic sums of the state matrix. If the adjoint generator is diagonal on the matrix units, the spectral classes inside the residue classes of the index difference modulo the register dimension $M$ give a constructive basis, an exact dimension formula, and attainable bounds: the dimension of the visible space lies between $M$ and $M^2-M+1$.

The class includes independent qubit dephasing, and an analytically solvable reference model of Gorini--Kossakowski--Lindblad--Sudarshan (GKLS) type yields a damped Fejér kernel; two random-unitary channels with the same Ramsey contrast show that higher harmonics are distinguishable in the QPE distribution. For approximate reduction we use a finite-time Gramian and an a posteriori residual estimate, with a quadratic error order for a reducing unperturbed subspace and a compatible initial state.

Numerical calculations check the consistency of the representations and the behaviour of the error under non-Toeplitz perturbations.

items.title: InterQ-RL: Interaction-Aware Correction of Execution Mismatch in Quantized Agentic RL
items.summary:
Multi-turn agent reinforcement learning (RL) relies on long closed-loop rollouts, making generation and KV-cache costs a major bottleneck. Quantized rollout reduces these costs, but its low-precision executor also serves as the behavior policy and can induce execution mismatch with the learner.

Existing quantized-RL methods are designed primarily for single-turn generation. They align the learner forward with quantized rollout or correct the current-token rollout-learner ratio, without modeling the policy history that produces each agent state.

Even after quantization alignment, residual rollout-learner mismatch accumulates along the state-reaching policy history, so a current action may look locally aligned despite a mismatched history. We introduce InterQ-RL (Interaction-aware Quantized Reinforcement Learning) to correct this post-alignment mismatch.

It applies bounded execution-prefix correction over the state-reaching policy history, allocates correction strength across action segments by effective support under a fixed displacement budget, and requires no additional model forward pass. We evaluate dense and mixture-of-experts (MoE) backbones from 4B to 30B on ALFWorld, WebShop, and ScienceWorld, with all quantized arms sharing the same rollout with 8-bit weights, activations, and KV cache (W8A8-KV8).

Across four environment-backbone settings, InterQ-RL achieves the strongest quantized endpoint result, matching BF16 to within 0.7 points and exceeding it in two settings. It matches or exceeds the learning speed of alignment alone while avoiding its late performance regression.

items.title: Let the Gate Decide: Per-Lookup Precision for Quantized Conditional Memory in LLMs
items.summary:
Conditional memory layers, such as DeepSeek's Engram, attach large hashed n-gram tables to a language model, and removing them from DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash costs 36.8 PopQA points. Low-bit quantization loses long-tail facts first, and the standard remedy, giving more bits to frequently accessed rows, backfires: refining lookups by access frequency is worse than refining them at random.

We trace this to the gate that scales each retrieved row. A lookup's quantization error is weighted by its gate, which is small for frequent n-grams, large for the rare n-grams of long-tail entities, and computable from a 1-bit code.

GateRQ therefore stores each row as a ladder of 1-bit residual codes, keeps level 1 in GPU memory to compute the gate, and reads deeper levels only for the lookups the gate ranks highest. Without retraining, GateRQ cuts GPU table memory by 7.8x on DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash, which raises vLLM throughput by 11%-31% over FP8 tables, while losing about 1 PopQA point at 1.50 bits read per lookup and 0.2 points at 2.10 bits across two models.

items.title: A Control Line Multiplexing Framework for Scalable Quantum Computing
items.summary:
Universal fault-tolerant superconducting quantum computers are expected to require millions of physical qubits; yet extending the prevailing dedicated-control-line paradigm to this scale would exceed the wiring density and cooling-power budget of dilution refrigerators. Microwave frequency-division multiplexing (FDM) revolutionized classical communications by enabling many independent channels to share common transmission infrastructure.

Translating this principle to superconducting quantum control, however, requires an all-microwave architecture and experimental validation of frequency-multiplexed gate control. Recent work in quantum error correction has demonstrated microwave-based readout, single-qubit gates and leakage suppression, whereas two-qubit gates remain predominantly driven by unipolar pulses and thus constitute the missing element of an all-microwave architecture.

Here, we propose a periodically extensible hybrid multiplexing framework in which all gate operations are frequency-division multiplexed using polychromatic microwave pulses and band-pass filters, thereby reducing the required control-line count by one to two orders of magnitude. In a 1:4 demonstration, we achieve average errors of $(6.4\pm0.2)\times10^{-3}$ for parallel FDM CZ gates and $(10.6\pm0.2)\times10^{-4}$ for parallel FDM $XY(π/2)$ gates, without statistically significant multiplexing-induced degradation.

Together with on-chip DC sources, this FDM-based gate-control scheme completes the last missing module in a scalable multiplexed-control architecture toward universal fault-tolerant quantum computing.

items.title: Ramdeobaba University and QClairvoyance Quantum Labs to Set Up Quantum Software and Quantum Communication Labs in Nagpur
items.summary:
Insider Brief

Ramdeobaba University and QClairvoyance Quantum Labs signed an agreement to establish quantum software and quantum communication hardware laboratories at the university’s Nagpur campus.

The laboratories will provide browser-based tools for developing quantum algorithms and hardware kits for quantum key distribution and quantum random number generation.

QClairvoyance will assign two qualified professionals to the university for 12 months, provide faculty training and support joint research, academic projects and internships.

Image: Photo by Onkarphoto on Unsplash

PRESS RELEASE — Ramdeobaba University (RBU), Nagpur, and QClairvoyance Quantum Labs Pvt. Ltd., a deep-tech startup based in Secunderabad, have signed a Memorandum of Understanding (MoU) to establish two specialised laboratories on the RBU campus: a quantum software lab and a quantum communication hardware lab.

The initiative aims to bring emerging quantum technologies into the classroom, giving students and faculty hands-on access to quantum computing and next-generation secure communication technologies. Through practical learning and research exposure, the collaboration will help students develop the skills and knowledge needed to understand and work with these technologies as they evolve.

items.title: DTCA: Denoising Token Credit Assignment for Reinforcement Learning in Diffusion Language Models
items.summary:
Diffusion language models (DLMs) generate text through iterative denoising, enabling bidirectional context modeling and parallel token refinement. Recent studies have applied reinforcement learning (RL) to DLMs and improved their reasoning performance.

However, the iterative denoising process makes credit assignment more challenging, as final outcome rewards provide limited information about how different tokens contribute to the final output. In this paper, we propose Denoising Token Credit Assignment (DTCA), a framework for token-level credit assignment in reinforcement learning for diffusion language models.

DTCA estimates token contributions by measuring the improvement in prediction confidence of remaining masked positions after token commitment and groups these signals according to part-of-speech (POS) categories. These contribution weights are used to select informative denoising timesteps and assign token-level learning signals during RL training.

DTCA further calibrates these learning signals according to token-level entropy changes induced by policy updates. Experiments on LLaDA-8B-Instruct show that DTCA consistently improves mathematical reasoning performance across different generation budgets, with gains of up to 9.0 points on MATH500 and 5.3 points on GSM8K over the base model.

items.title: Self-Correcting 3D Surface Code with Growing Local Dimension
items.summary:
We construct self-correcting 3D surface codes over $\mathbb Z_q$ with local dimension $q$ growing with system size. The model preserves the local geometry and stabilizer support of the ordinary 3D surface code and remains translation invariant in the bulk, while modifying only the stabilizer Pauli powers.

We use the Lee metric to characterize error weight and consider local Metropolis dynamics with single-qudit $X^{\pm1}$ and $Z^{\pm1}$ updates, each changing the energy by at most a constant independent of $q$ and system size $N$. We prove that, below the critical temperature, when the local dimension scales as $q=Θ(N)$, the memory times in both error sectors grow at least as $\exp\left[Ω(N^{1/3})\right]$.

Our numerical results further support these analytical results. Together, these results establish growing local Hilbert-space dimension as a new resource for designing self-correcting quantum memories while retaining simple local geometry and local thermal dynamics.

items.title: Sharp effective Nullstellensatz for projective Cohen-Macaulay schemes
items.summary:
In this paper, we prove a sharp effective Nullstellensatz for projective Cohen-Macaulay schemes of pure dimension over an arbitrary field. In particular, if L is an ample line bundle on a smooth complex projective variety X and J is a coherent ideal sheaf with J\otimes L globally generated, then (\sqrt{J})^{°_L X}\subseteq J.

This establishes the sharp bound conjectured by Ein and Lazarsfeld. More generally, we obtain sharp bounds in terms of mixed intersection numbers and a refinement involving products of powers of prime ideal sheaves associated to the irreducible components of the base locus.

We also establish sharp radical power bounds for homogeneous ideals in finitely generated standard graded Cohen-Macaulay domains, extending Kollár's sharp effective Nullstellensatz for polynomial rings. The proofs combine purity and cycle preservation for leading Ext sheaves with Koszul evaluation maps compatible with successive divisor cuts.

items.title: Qubit’s Own Electric Current Could Offer a Simpler Readout Method
items.summary:
Insider Brief

Researchers proposed a method for reading Andreev qubits through their own oscillating supercurrent, potentially reducing measurement disturbance and eliminating auxiliary qubits.

The approach would use a sensitive magnetic detector to track the current and reconstruct the qubit’s state without requiring repeated resets.

Simulations reported reconstruction accuracies of 99.52% to 99.85%, but the proposed setup has yet to be tested experimentally.

Image: Photo by A Chosen Soul on Unsplash

PRESS RELEASE — One of the fundamental challenges of quantum computing is obtaining information from a quantum bit, or qubit. Unlike a conventional bit, which can be read repeatedly without altering its content, direct measurement of a quantum system typically causes the state to collapse before it can be determined. In other words, reading the information modifies it.

A new study with support from FAPESP proposes circumventing this problem by utilizing a unique property of a certain type of qubit called an “Andreev qubit.” This qubit produces an oscillating electric supercurrent through its own quantum dynamics. This supercurrent would serve as a macroscopic indicator of the qubit’s state, enabling its reconstruction in a virtually non-destructive manner.

items.title: End-to-End MXFP8 Reinforcement Learning on Blackwell: What Matching Buys, When It Pays Off, and How It Fails
items.summary:
Low-precision arithmetic can make reinforcement learning (RL) for large language models cheaper, but RL requires the sampler and the learner to agree. Several frameworks now run FP8 on both sides. We implement end-to-end MXFP8 RL in verl (Megatron/Transformer Engine training; vLLM and SGLang rollout; dense and MoE models) and measure on B200 GPUs, with Qwen3-8B and Qwen3-30B-A3B, what this design buys, when it is faster, and how it fails.

(1) Matching.
